#6668. A Complete Timeline of Justin and Hailey Bieber’s Relationship

The singer and supermodel-turned-skin care mogul are one of Hollywood’s leading power couples.

Justin Bieber and Hailey Baldwin dated on and off long before they became husband and wife. Hailey first met Justin in the late aughts, and they eventually struck up a casual romance.

Though they decided to keep it out of the public eye, this didn’t stop fans from obsessing over their relationship. After a breakup and surprise reconciliation-turned-whirlwind engagement two years later, Justin officially made Hailey his Mrs. during a September 2018 New York City courthouse ceremony. They got married in front of friends and family in a more formal wedding a year later. In May 2024, they announced they were expecting their first child. They welcomed their son, Jack, in August 2024.

From their highly publicized South Carolina nuptials to their adjustment to parenthood, here’s the couple’s full history and how their relationship has evolved.

Hailey has her father, Stephen, to thank for introducing her to her future husband. There’s even footage of their first meeting, which took place backstage at The Today Show. Hailey and Justin—then in their teens—shared a brief handshake and the rest, as they say, is history.

Chaperoned by her father yet again, Hailey attended the New York City premiere of Justin’s documentary Never Say Never. Later that month, Justin confirmed his relationship with Selena Gomez when the couple made their red carpet debut at Vanity Fair’s Oscar After Party.

Hailey officially declared herself a member of the Jelena fan club. The model took to Twitter, sharing her support for the couple. “I don’t care what anyone says but Justin Bieber and Selena Gomez together is the definition of a teenage dream! #word,” Hailey wrote.

After calling it quits with Gomez, Justin was photographed attending church services at Hillsong alongside Hailey and fellow supermodel Kendall Jenner. It wasn’t long before fans began speculating that Hailey and Justin were an item.

Hailey denied any romantic connection between her and Justin. She set the record straight during an interview with E!. “I’ve known [Justin] since I was like 13—and we’ve just been good friends over the years,” Hailey said. “We have just stayed close, and there’s nothing more to it than that.”

Justin backed up Hailey’s statement in an Instagram post. The singer shared a snap of himself and Hailey, writing, “I’m super single and this is my good friend u would know otherwise.”

Hailey joined Justin and his family on vacation in Anguilla, fueling rumors that their friendship was actually something more.

Justin made his romance with Hailey Instagram official. Shortly after New Year’s Day, he shared a photo of them kissing.

Hailey and Justin revealed that their relationship was casual. “We are not an exclusive couple,” Hailey told E!. Meanwhile, in an interview with GQ, Justin called Hailey “someone I really love,” but he added that he didn’t “want to be held down by anything.”

Hailey and Justin ended their brief fling. According to People, Justin also unfollowed Hailey on Instagram amid his new relationship with Sofia Richie.

Following their split, Hailey and Justin completely lost touch for almost two years. In 2020, Hailey shared her thoughts on their time apart: “Our lives seemed to be going in very different directions,” she told ELLE. “I actually think—now that I look back at it being married—that it was a good thing for the two of us, very healthy.”

During Justin and Hailey’s rift, the singer rekindled his romance with Gomez in November 2017. However, by March 2018, Jelena was over for good.

Hailey revealed that she was speaking to Justin again. “We went through a long period of time when we weren’t friends,” she told The Times U.K.. “We’ve moved past that.”

Justin and Hailey appeared as if they were back together. After sharing some PDA at a religious conference, they were spotted together at LIV nightclub in Miami. Just days later, they were photographed holding hands and kissing in New York City.

After rumors of the couple’s engagement began to swirl, Justin confirmed the news on Instagram. He posted two portraits with his new fiancée and penned a lengthy caption devoted to her. “Hailey I am soooo in love with everything about you,” he wrote. “So committed to spending my life getting to know every single part of you.”

Hailey joined the love fest, tweeting, “Not sure what I did in life to deserve such happiness but I am so utterly grateful to God for giving me such an incredible person to share my life with!”

Just two months after their engagement, TMZ ran photographs of the couple walking into New York City’s Marriage Bureau. The next day, People claimed that Hailey and Justin obtained their marriage license, officially making them husband and wife.

Meanwhile, Hailey dismissed the gossip on Twitter: “I understand where the speculation is coming from, but I’m not married yet!”

The couple finally confirmed their marriage status. Justin shared an Instagram photo of him and Hailey with the caption “My wife is awesome.” The following day, Hailey changed her last name to Bieber on all of her social media accounts.

TMZ broke the news that a second wedding was imminent after the date was moved several times. The outlet acquired a photo of a save the date card, which revealed that the ceremony would take place on September 30 in South Carolina.

Mr. and Mrs. Bieber officially tied the knot…again! People disclosed the details of their ceremony, which took place at Somerset Chapel in Bluffton, South Carolina. Vows (and Tiffany & Co. wedding bands) were exchanged “as the sun set.” The star-studded guest list included Kendall Jenner, Camila Morrone, and Jaden Smith, among others.

A day later, Justin basked in wedded bliss as he shared photos from the couple’s reception.

The Biebers continued to share photos from their big day. Hailey put her Off-White by Virgil Abloh wedding dress on full display, including her elaborate train, which read “’till death do us part.” Justin wore a Celine tuxedo.

Weeks later, the newlyweds found themselves embroiled in Jelena fan drama, after Justin’s ex dropped her new single “Lose You To Love Me.” The track captured Gomez’s feelings moving on from her 10-year on-off romance with Justin and closing that chapter.

Shortly after the song came out, Hailey upset some Jelena fans when she posted an Instagram Story, where she shared that she was listening to Summer Walker’s “I’ll Kill You.” Hailey denied that this was a dig at Gomez. Commenting beneath JustJared’s Instagram post, she wrote, “please stop with this nonsense. There is no ‘response.’ This is complete BS.”

Gomez, meanwhile, told her fans on Instagram Live not to attack Hailey. “I am grateful for the response that the song is getting. I’m so grateful,” she said. “However, I do not stand for women tearing women down. And I will never, ever be by that. So please be kind to everyone. It doesn’t matter what the situation is. If you’re my fans, don’t be rude to anybody, please. Don’t go off and say things that you just feel in the moment. And just please, from me, know that that’s not my heart. My heart is only to release things that I feel that are me and that I’m proud of. And that’s all that I’ll say, yeah.”

Hailey tried to shut down feud rumors herself when she liked Gomez’s Instagram post promoting “Lose You To Love Me.” A source close to the Biebers also assured E! that things were copacetic. “It isn’t ideal for Hailey,” the insider told the outlet, “but she understands the creative process of writing music and that Justin had a past. Justin and Hailey both want Selena to be happy and in a good place and aren’t fazed by it.”

Justin rang in the decade with his new single “Yummy,” which details his sex life with Hailey.

Hailey landed the March 2020 cover of ELLE. She spoke candidly about the couple’s decision to delay their South Carolina ceremony for a year. “When we first got married, we were just figuring out our life together,” she said. “I felt like putting a wedding in the middle of all of that would be really hectic and stressful.”

Although the Biebers weren’t ready for children yet, Hailey was already thinking about parenting. Amid worldwide protests in solidarity with Black Lives Matter, Hailey discussed her outlook on motherhood. Regarding her future children, she told Vogue India, “They will be raised knowing how to treat people, why we don’t say certain things, and why we respect and acknowledge and give credit where credit is due.”

The Biebers attended their first Met Gala as husband and wife. Hailey stunned in a Saint Laurent column gown and matching wayfarer sunglasses. Justin paired his sleek suit with customized Nike sneakers.

Hailey and Justin appeared on the In Good Faith with Chelsea & Judah Smith podcast, where they discussed the challenges they faced in their first year of marriage. At the time, Justin was battling with severe bouts of depression. Hailey admitted that watching her partner struggle wasn’t easy.

“There were days where I literally was like, ‘I don’t know if he’s going to be okay.’ Something really deep down inside of me was like, ‘He’s going to get through it.’ I just didn’t know how long it was going to take. That’s what I think was the hardest thing. There’s no guarantees,” she said.

Nevertheless, Hailey was determined to stick by her husband: “Imagine abandoning somebody in the middle of the worst time of their life, potentially. I’m not that type of person,” she said.

Amid the launch of her skin care line Rhode, Hailey did an interview with WSJ Magazine. The entrepreneur shared her thoughts on having children. “I think ideally in the next couple of years we would try. But there’s a reason they call it try, right?” she said. “You don’t know how long that process is ever going to take. Definitely no kids this year; that would be a little bit hectic, I think.”

Hailey also revealed her decision to stop discussing her marriage in interviews. “It doesn’t feel worth it to me anymore,” she explained. “I try to have an open conversation with someone, and then it gets taken out of context.”

Hailey was hospitalized after having stroke-like symptoms, though she fortunately fully recovered. Her health scare left Justin reasonably shaken, with a source close to the couple telling People, “[He] is probably more traumatized than even she is. When it happened, there was a lot of panic. Justin texted everyone he knew and asked everyone to pray for her, and he never left her side. He was saying that he can’t lose her, that whatever it takes, he wanted the best medical treatment available.”

Justin later discussed the situation during one of his concerts. “You know, it’s kind of crazy how life throws you curveballs,” he said during a Denver performance. “Most of you probably know or seen the news about my wife …but she’s okay, she’s good, she’s strong. It’s been really scary. But I know for a fact that God has her in the palms of his hands, and that’s a good thing.”

Hailey accompanied her husband at the Grammys. She opted for a flowy strapless gown, which led some fans to speculate that she was hiding a growing baby bump. After RadarOnline published an Instagram post about the rumors, Hailey swiftly shut them down. “I’m not pregnant; leave me alone,” she commented.

Just months after Hailey’s hospitalization, Justin had a health scare of his own. A virus called Ramsay Hunt syndrome left half of the singer’s face paralyzed, but he eventually recovered. A source told People that although this year has been “overwhelming” for the couple, relationship-wise, “they’re unbreakable.”

During an interview with Good Morning America, Hailey shared a promising update on her husband’s health. “He is getting better every single day. He’s feeling a lot better and, obviously, it was just a very scary and random situation to happen, but he’s going to be totally okay, and I’m just grateful that he’s fine,” she said.

Ahead of the couple’s fourth anniversary, Hailey discussed her relationship with Justin in Harper’s Bazaar. “[Justin’s] still the person that I wanna be rushing back to,” she said. “I might fly somewhere and go do a job, but I can’t wait to come back and hang out. And I feel like that’s because of the effort that’s been put in on both sides. At the end of the day, like, he’s my best friend, but it still does take a lot of work to make it work.”

Hailey appeared on the Call Her Daddy podcast. In a conversation with Alexandra Cooper, Hailey insisted that she never “stole” Justin from Gomez and that it’s “not [her] character to mess with someone’s relationship.” She also confirmed that Justin had already “closed a chapter” with Gomez before he rekindled things with her in 2018.

Hailey went on to discuss her seemingly speedy engagement to Justin, which took place just two months after they began dating again. “I’m like, ‘yeah, that seemed really drastic and really crazy,’” she said. “But that was what we felt was a decision between the two of us, and it felt correct for the two of us at the time, and clearly, we were right because here we are, four years later.”

Hailey and Gomez posed for pictures together at the Academy Museum Gala, proving once and for all that there is no drama between them. Of Hailey and Gomez’s motivation, a source told Entertainment Tonight, “Selena and Hailey were both super chill together at the Academy Museum Gala. They’ve both moved on and are happy in their own lives. They wanted to show the world that there’s no beef or bad feelings between them anymore.”

A source gave Entertainment Tonight a brief update on Hailey and Justin’s relationship as 2022 closed out. “Hailey and Justin are doing incredible as a couple,” the source said. “They are each other’s rocks. “They have so much love and passion in their relationship and share the same beliefs and values, so it’s easy for them to get along,” the insider continued. “They love doing pretty much everything together, especially traveling.” The couple ended their year by traveling to Aspen and celebrating the start of 2023 with Kendall and Kylie Jenner.

My favorite thing about being married is honestly the companionship I feel we have,” she said. “Genuinely, you are my best friend in the entire world. #6667. A Look Back at Legendary Kennedy Family Parties, on JFK Jr.’s Birthday

Today would have been the late John F. Kennedy Jr.’s 66th birthday—and his celebration would undoubtedly have been a gleaming affair, much like his iconic wedding to Carolyn Bessette was in 1996. In fact, it seems that the Kennedy clan never met a party they didn’t like, especially when it came to close-knit family celebrations in Washington, D.C., and at their compound on the Cape.

Perhaps the most famous—or infamous, rather—event of the Kennedys was JFK’s birthday celebration at Madison Square Garden in 1962. It was a Democratic fundraiser-slash-birthday salute, where Marilyn Monroe sang her sultry “Happy birthday, Mr. President” in a skin-tight dress (in 2016, the dress sold at auction for $4.8 million).

But there were also more tame affairs like JFK Jr. and Caroline’s balloon-and toy-bedecked birthday parties in the White House when they were children, and a surprise celebration for President Kennedy thrown by his White House staff. Over the years, there have been fundraisers (including one where President Kennedy sat with Frank Sinatra), weddings, family gatherings at the Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port, Fourth of July reunions, and more.

Here, a look back at some of the most memorable parties and events in the Kennedy family’s history.

At a party being held in honor of Jean Kennedy, sister of Democratic Senator John Kennedy. Left to right seated: Jacqueline Kennedy; Patricia Lawford; Ethel Kennedy; Eunice Shrivers. Standing: Jean Kennedy.

John Kennedy, Jacqueline Kennedy, and their wedding party in 1953 at Hammersmith Farm in Newport after the wedding.

Quentin N. Burdick and John F. Kennedy at his birthday party. June 1960.

Then Senator John F Kennedy and entertainer Frank Sinatra attend a black tie, Democratic Committee Dinner at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, Los Angeles, California, July 10, 1960.

Marilyn Monroe singing “Happy Birthday” to John F. Kennedy at the Democratic rally for his birthday. May 19, 1962.

Marilyn Monroe between Robert and John F. Kennedy at the party following the Democratic rally for his birthday. May 19, 1962.

Steven E. Smith, brother-in-law of U.S. President John F. Kennedy, visiting with actress Marilyn Monroe during reception at the residence of Arthur B. Krim and Dr. Mathilde Krim, New York City.

A joint birthday party for Caroline Kennedy and John F. Kennedy, Jr. November 27, 1962.

A joint birthday party for Caroline Kennedy and John F. Kennedy, Jr. November 27, 1962.

John F. Kennedy’s White House birthday party. May 28, 1963.

President Kennedy and the First Lady, and Vice President and Mrs. Lyndon B. Johnson pose for pictures shortly after arriving at the National Guard Armory in January 1962.

A joint birthday celebration for Caroline and John F. Kennedy, Jr., in the White House screening room. The party was postponed by JFK’s death and was held on the family’s last day in the White House. December 5, 1963.

John F. Kennedy, Jr., eating ice cream at a birthday party. February 1963.

Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis with her younger sister, Lee Radziwill, at party in December 1972, thrown in honor of Radziwill by Ladies' Home Journal.

Members of the Kennedy family chat during a gathering at the Kennedy compound in 1980.

Three members of the Kennedy family at the official groundbreaking ceremony for the John Fitzgerald Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum in Boston, Massachusetts, 12th June 1977. From left, John F. Kennedy Jr., his sister Caroline Kennedy, and their mother, Jacqueline Kennedy.

In May 1967, nine-year-old Caroline Kennedy christened a ship in honor of her father.

Kennedy family at Thanksgiving at Hyannisport, Massachusetts, 1948. From left: John F. Kennedy, Jean Ann Smith, Rose Kennedy, Joseph Kennedy Sr., Patricia Lawford, Robert F. Kennedy, Eunice Mary Shriver, Edward Kennedy.

#6666. 25 Midwestern Thanksgiving Recipes That Bring The Nostalgia (& The Flavor)

Even nicer than Midwest nice (and that's saying something!).

My holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. With my mom’s Alabama and Texas roots and my dad's Missouri and Kansas roots, that meant that Christmas dinner was a Southern affair and Thanksgiving was a Midwestern feast. Both holiday spreads had a fair amount of overlap of dishes (casseroles galore), but I have to say: A classic Midwest Thanksgiving has a special place in my heart.

What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:

Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

It takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. It’s for those that want to feel like they are putting some effort into their appetizer without it being difficult or time-consuming.

Don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

For this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. It's not how my mom makes it, but trust me—by sautéing mushrooms with sliced onion in butter, you're building a base with some serious depth of flavor. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

No matter the holiday, one thing is for sure: Deviled eggs will be making an appearance. Variations are always welcome (looking at you, harissa deviled eggs), but if grandpa is going to have a happy Thanksgiving, then this classic recipe better be present.

Strawberry pretzel tart, AKA strawberry pretzel salad, might sound a little strange, but trust us—it strikes the perfect balance of whimsical and classic, sweet and salty. The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

We’re certainly not opposed to roasted Brussels sprouts, but we also love giving them the traditional Thanksgiving treatment—plenty of butter, cream, and cheese. This method upgrades even the most humble vegetables while still allowing them to be the star of the show.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for. Plus, you can easily make it ahead and travel with it, making it an ideal potluck recipe.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. The hollowed-out potatoes are an excellent vessel for extra-creamy mashed potatoes, stuffing, turkey, and dollops of cranberry sauce.

Essentially, this is chicken Alfredo, but with a few extra decadent add-ins, like cream cheese, garlic, and punchy spices like nutmeg and black pepper. When you’re craving the classic but have to serve a crowd, this is the recipe you should make.

A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a new, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

I'll clarify that when I say stuffing, I'm actually referring to dressing. Traditional stuffing should be stuffed inside the turkey and cooked in there, but in my family, we've always called it stuffing. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath.

What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato, of course. With this in mind, we combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

Most sweet potato casseroles have only marshmallows or pecans. Don't even think about making this mistake. Topping with a pecan streusel and then marshmallows helps this Thanksgiving casserole stand out above all the rest.

If you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with a wildly satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

Step aside, all other casseroles—corn is not to be overlooked on the holiday table. If you prefer, drained and rinsed canned corn can be used instead of frozen, and you could substitute more milk in for the heavy cream. The finished casserole won't be quite as decadent, but it will still be delicious.

Deviled eggs are great, but when you have them for every holiday, it just makes sense to change them up sometimes. These are our new obsession

If green beans dressed up as cheesy garlic bread, then they would become these Parmesan roasted green beans. Tossed in garlic and black pepper and showered with cheese, this simply irresistible side dish will steal the spotlight at every holiday table.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for.

The actor joined Jimmy Fallon in an embellished runway piece

Florals... for fall? While not quite groundbreaking, per say, the pattern is certainly not as common during the chilly months as it might be in the springtime. But leave it to Amanda Seyfried to show us how it’s done.

For an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, the actor wore a black Carolina Herrera midi dress that, despite being from Wes Gordon’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection, felt like an appropriate choice for November.

The Mamma Mia! actor joined Fallon for a conversation about how she got involved in Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything. “It was never my intention to recreate Elizabeth Holmes ever again,” Seyfried, who previously portrayed the Theranos founder in biopic series The Dropout, told the host. “But Nathan Fielder, the director, reached out and said, ‘Hey, I’d love to pick your brain.’”

Continuing, she revealed that the two talked on FaceTime for an hour, before Fielder asked if she would be comfortable being filmed watching the footage. “A couple weeks later, I was watching the footage with four cameras in my apartment,” she revealed. “I was like, ‘How did I get here?’”

#6664. An All-Time Great Air Jordan Is Returning on Black Friday

Sit still for a second. The birds are singing. The sun is shining. The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning. Nature is healing. Everything, for once, is exactly where it should be.

The ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989. Created by legendary Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, it came in slick black nubuck with hits of gray and red throughout. Michael Jordan famously wore a pair when he hit The Shot over Craig Ehlo to knock the Cleveland Cavaliers out of the 1989 NBA Playoffs—so, yeah, there’s a bit of lore there too.

Unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years. There was a retro in 1999, followed by versions in 2008 and 2012, and then another in 2019, which finally brought the OG “Nike Air” branding back to the heel. Then, in 2024, we got the ‘Bred Reimagined,’ which swapped the classic nubuck for leather. The less said about that one, the better.

Because two years later, Jordan Brand is going back to the good stuff. The ‘Bred’ is decked out in black nubuck again, with gray eyelets, red accents around the sole, and the all-important “Nike Air” stamped across the back. Even the Nike branding on the outsole is returning. Basically, if you looked at the ‘Bred Reimagined’ and thought, “Look how they massacred my boy,” congrats: this one's for you.

And there’s something quite nice about that. The AJ4 has been messed with, remixed, collabed on, and reworked in just about every way possible over the last few years. Some of those experiments have been great! Some… not so much. The ‘Bred’ doesn’t really need any of that. It’s been one of the best Air Jordans on the planet for 37 years. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is set to drop on November 27 via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists globally.

#6662. Mascara Has Entered Its Sophisticated Era

Of all the products in our makeup bags, mascara might be the one to which we’re most loyal. Most of us found a formula we liked years ago, kept buying it, and never looked back. In the interim, foundations went matte and then glowy, skincare got upgraded with peptides and NAD+, and lipstick shade ranges have grown exponentially. Mascara on the other hand has worked pretty much the same: a fluffy blush dipped in rich black pigment.

That is, until now. The humble mascara is undergoing something of a renaissance. Tubing technologies promise effortless removal; long-wear formulas rival their longwear counterparts in the smudge department; rich browns and burgundies offer colorful alternative to the expected onyx; and meticulously engineered wands deliver the sort of precision even a makeup minimalist would love.

The reality is that mascara just works better now. The new formulas don’t flake by the afternoon or smudge into dark circles, and you can take them off without losing a bunch of lashes in the process. “I want my lashes to look beautiful at 9 a.m. and still look intentional at 9 p.m.,” says celebrity makeup artist Nam Vo. “I don’t need to check my under-eyes every 20 minutes.”

Ahead, makeup artists and industry experts explain what’s actually new, what’s just marketing, and the mascaras worth buying now.

A lot of the change comes down to what we want our lashes to look like. For years, the best mascara was the one that made lashes as big and black as possible, clumps and all. “I think mascara has finally entered its sophisticated era,” says Vo. “We’re moving away from just wanting huge, thick, spider-leg lashes and toward precision, separation, lift, and definition.” Anthonino Olimpio, a global beauty marketing executive and professor at Parsons School of Design, has noticed the same thing. “Now everyone wants intensity, with separated, fluttery lashes that make people ask, ‘Wait, are those yours?’” he says.

That doesn’t mean everyone wants the same thing. On Pinterest, both ends of the spectrum are growing at once. “Searches for ‘full beat makeup looks’ have increased 460%, while ‘soft natural makeup looks’ are up 105% and ‘soft wispy lashes’ have risen 199%,” says Sydney Stanback, Pinterest’s global head of trends and insights. People are also searching for much more specific looks. “People are becoming increasingly specific in their searches, looking beyond general eye makeup inspiration to particular lash shapes, styles and techniques,” she says. Olimpio sees it in how people put their mascara on. “People are lash mapping, going wispy on the outer corners and defined on the inner, and bottom lashes are officially back,” he says. “I’m a guy, and I wear a light coat most days. A sheer, natural lash is for everyone now.”

The products have changed quite a bit, too, starting with the wand. “Brushes are the real heroes here,” says Olimpio. “Molded elastomer wands let developers engineer exactly where every bristle sits, so you’re designing the lash instead of praying for it.” Pro makeup artist Tatevik Saghyan points to smaller, curved wands that can reach the shortest lashes in the inner and outer corners without clumping. Olimpio is also a fan of a part most people never notice. “And my nerdy favorite detail is the wiper inside the tube. It’s the unsung hero,” he says. “It decides how much product actually reaches the brush, and better wipers mean fewer clumps before you’ve even started.”

Tubing has also taken over in 2026. Instead of coating lashes in a wax-based formula, tubing mascaras wrap each one in a flexible polymer sleeve that slides off with warm water. “Tubing is the real deal,” says Olimpio. Celebrity makeup artist Kasey Spicard uses it on almost everyone she works with. “I almost exclusively use tubing mascaras on my clients,” she says. It also fixed something most people had just put up with. “The great betrayal of mascara was making us choose,” says Olimpio. “Either it lasted all day and you practically needed a chisel to take it off, or it came off easily and you had raccoon eyes by lunch. That trade-off is finally dead.”

Some newer formulas are coming from Asia, too. “Emerging now is growth in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese mascara formulas, with brands like Judydoll and Dolly Wink that have longwear mascaras that don’t make the lashes go straight,” says Spicard. “Once you curl your lashes, the curl stays, or the formula helps curl the lash itself.” Plus, colored mascara has made its return, but it’s not the electric blue of the early 2000s. Now it’s deep burgundy, navy and plum. “It’s color, but make it expensive,” says Vo.

So, you don’t need the biggest lashes or the most impressive claims on the tube, just the one that suits your lashes and still looks good when you get home. Below, a few of our favorites that we think are worth buying.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts— celebrity and pro makeup artists—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to mascaras, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, wand shape, benefits, whether it’s waterproof, and additional features. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.

#6659. Popeyes Beat KFC In My Chicken Sandwich Showdown—But Can It Take Down Chick-fil-A?

The chicken sandwich wars are far from over.

Few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

In my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

My biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be said for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

Popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it launched in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

The mayo was another important part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

While Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

Chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

#6657. The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Plagued by the prospect of excess and loose skin, one writer investigates the surgical and noninvasive options that lie ahead

I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery. Weight loss has been on my mind basically my entire life, especially since I started this journey in earnest in July 2019. And, as proud of myself as I most certainly am for losing this weight and finally getting healthier, it is met toe-to-toe with pervasive anxiety and a nagging question: What about excess skin?

Because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go. I worry, perhaps too much, about whether I’ll make it to my goal weight without needing skin tightening at the end of this journey.

It’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed. But for those like me who are on major weight-loss journeys, or whose bodies have changed significantly through pregnancy, it’s a question that plagues us: Am I going to encounter excess skin the more weight I lose? And if I do, what can I do about it?

Apparently, I’m not the only one with questions, according to New York City plastic surgeon Lara Devgan. “Skin tightening remains one of the elusive black boxes in the world of plastic surgery,” she says. That said, we’re all still learning about best practices—from me to medical professionals.

So I decided to dig deeper. I rounded up five renowned dermatologists and plastic surgeons from across the country and asked them my questions. And here’s what they have to say.

“Losing weight gradually rather than rapidly may prevent excess skin after major weight loss,” says Los Angeles–based dermatologist Harold Lancer. “However, rapid large-scale weight loss will invariably result in excess skin.” Devgan seconds that. “The best way to prevent skin laxity after weight loss is to do your best to lose weight at a slow and steady pace,” she says. “Although it may sound appealing to get to the finish line quickly, that is actually the worst thing you can do in terms of skin laxity.” Losing weight slowly, she says, allows the skin to contract and shrink as the body shape changes.

Though I personally haven’t opted for weight loss surgery, many do—and there is zero shame in that. But because weight is lost more rapidly after surgery, the likelihood of excess skin increases, so experts recommend pairing weight loss surgery with a skin removal procedure. Why worry about excess skin, especially after faster weight loss? It’s “because collagen and elastin fibers are destroyed when skin is stretched significantly and remains stretched for an extended amount of time,” says New York City plastic surgeon David Shafer. “Patients should plan on staged procedures if having a weight loss surgery followed by a skin removal surgery.”

“Typically, younger patients with thicker and more sebaceous skin will have more skin contraction during weight loss due to better elasticity,” Devgan says. “Starting in the 20s, tissue elasticity begins to decline. Even in the absence of weight fluctuation, loss of tissue turgor and decreased firmness can be seen in midface descent in the late 20s, breast laxity in the 30s, abdominal laxity in the 40s, and extremity laxity in the 50s.”

However, Devgan says everyone’s body is different. “There is a tremendous amount of variability in the human experience, so some patients may lose 50 pounds with minimal change in their body, while others can lose as few as 10 and see tissue laxity.” If you are genetically blessed with unusually superb tissue elasticity, Devgan says, it can be less dramatic. (And lucky you.)

Lifestyle choices can also factor in, Boston-based dermatologist Ranella Hirsch says. How long were you at the weight you started losing from? Are you a smoker? Do you spend a lot of time in the sun without protection? All these factors play into skin elasticity.

“Using an emollient moisturizer rich in vitamin E will help improve the barrier protection of the skin and lock in moisture,” Devgan says. She also says the topical medical-grade ingredients you use on your face for firmness and tightness—like hyaluronic acid, peptides, niacin, squalene, vitamins C and B, retinol, and bakuchiol—can work elsewhere, too. “Most people focus on using these for the face and neck in their daily routines, but from a molecular perspective, their efficacy is present anywhere on the body.” But save your money on creams that promise you the world. “Losing large amounts of weight rapidly tends to leave skin behind,” Hirsch says. “Though creams with incredible claims abound, they actually do little.”

Biossance Squalane + Caffeine Toning Body Cream

Sol de Janeiro Bom Dia Bright Body Cream with Vitamin C

U Beauty The SCULPT Arm Compound Body Serum

Building muscle through weight training might help reduce the appearance of lax skin, New York City dermatologist Dendy Engelman says. “This helps reduce the appearance by replacing the lost fat with muscle mass.”

Nonsurgical options can help with loose skin after weight loss, but they won’t help with skin folds or hanging skin. “Noninvasive treatments such as laser and radiofrequency can help tighten the skin, but there is a limit to how much they can do,” Shafer adds. “Hanging skin generally needs to be surgically excised with procedures such as abdominoplasty, body lift, and arm lift.” Shafer says there’s a difference between loose skin and hanging skin. “It’s possible patients can manage and treat excess skin cases without undergoing skin removal surgery, such as if the skin is loose but not hanging.” He adds, “In that case, noninvasive treatments may be useful, but hanging skin most often requires surgical excision.”

“After major weight loss, people may have skin that hangs off their body,” Engelman says. “These heavy folds can cause health problems such as pain, inflammation, and frequent infections from the skin constantly rubbing together. This can happen during exercise or everyday activities. When a person is having functional issues because of their excess skin, it should be a sign that this problem needs to be addressed.” And, of course, everyone’s journey is different.

Lancer says some individuals will tolerate moderate laxity and be happy with the weight-loss accomplishment; others will seek skin tightening for as little as a five-pound weight loss. But, he says, if plastic surgery does become the option on the table, “I would recommend getting at least three opinions from doctors who exclusively do excess body skin reduction. Once you select a doctor, do one small area on your body, so you can evaluate the procedure, how your body heals, and your results. Afterward, you can determine whether you’d like to proceed with a full-blown larger procedure.”

He suggests consulting a dermatologist for nonsurgical options, then asking that doctor to recommend plastic surgeons who specialize in excess body skin reduction if you feel that is the right path for you. This is a major decision and shouldn’t be taken lightly. Bring medical professionals along for the entire weight-loss journey (even if you’ve already started) and ask all the questions: Which specific procedure is best? How much will it cost? Will insurance cover it? (From my research so far, no, if it is cosmetic, but perhaps yes if it would help correct something that limits your daily functionality.) No question is off-limits, and don’t try to make these decisions alone.

If this piece applies to you at all, whether it’s longstanding weight you carried, weight you lost during pregnancy, or somewhere in between, that means one thing: You’ve taken major steps toward better physical health, and that should be applauded. “Everyone’s weight loss story is different, and some days are harder than others,” Engelman says. “I say, try to be kind to yourself. You’ve just reached a huge accomplishment and should be proud of that.”

Devgan agrees. “Accomplishing a personal health goal like major weight loss is an incredible achievement that anyone should be proud of,” she says. “While excess skin can feel like a burden or source of self-consciousness, it is also a reminder of the metaphorical and literal shedding of the weight of a prior version of oneself. You cannot have a couture gown without a seam, and you cannot have a surgery without a scar. Life has limitations, but that does not make it less beautiful. It makes it more real.”

#6655. Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She says more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

#6654. 24 Veil Alternatives for the Bride Who’d Rather Skip Tradition

Some brides consider the wedding veil sacred, whether it’s an heirloom passed down through generations or a sweeping cathedral-length piece they’ve dreamed of since childhood. Others would rather skip tradition altogether, opting for a statement hair accessory in lieu of lace and tulle. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of veil alternatives—and while they’re a natural fit for courthouse weddings, elopements, and intimate vow exchanges, they can easily hold their own at more formal celebrations, too. Take Princess Eugenie, who ditched the veil entirely for her 2018 nuptials, letting a borrowed emerald tiara steal the show. (If a royal can forgo tradition, so can you!) More recently, Dua Lipa paired a custom Schiaparelli suit with a wide-brimmed Stephen Jones hat for her London civil ceremony.

Bridal designers are also going veil-free: Recent collections from Honor, Floure Studio, Vivienne Westwood, House of Gilles, and Elie Saab feature everything from sculptural hats to bows. When picking out your accessory for the big day, think about balance. An ivory headband adds a modern touch to an otherwise classic ball gown. A lace cloche dials up the drama on a minimalist dress, while a flowing, floral-embroidered scarf brings a romantic feel to a courthouse mini. Wearing a suit? A pillbox hat keeps things incredibly chic, whether you’re getting married at City Hall or eloping somewhere far-flung. Once you’ve settled on a style, be sure to bring it to your hair trial so your stylist knows how to incorporate your accessory seamlessly.

Ahead, discover 24 wedding veil alternatives for every type of bride.

Few accessories are as foolproof as a bridal headband, and with so many iterations on the market, it’s easy to find one that feels right for you. Unadorned padded styles from Loeffler Randall and Maison Ola draw instant attention to a low bun or sleek blowout, while a hand-embroidered option from Lock & Co. Hatters adds some sparkle.

If you’re planning a courthouse wedding or just want an accessory with real presence, a bridal hat is hard to beat. These wide-brimmed silhouettes from Maison Michel, Mains de Vapeur, and Eugenia Kim bring all the drama (and welcome shade at an outdoor ceremony). For something smaller, Gigi Burris’s pillbox has a lovely vintage-inspired aesthetic.

Juliet caps, cloches, and jeweled headpieces are heirlooms in the making; unlike delicate tulle, they’re sturdy enough to be passed down and worn again—plus, they have a built-in old-world feel. Alexandra Grecco and Jennifer Behr keep things soft with lace; De La Vali goes all out with a headscarf that drapes elegantly mid-back; Rabanne channels ’20s glamour with a pearl-and-bead design.

Not ready to surrender the movement of a veil? A cape or scarf offers a similar effect—just in a less conventional way. Rat & Boa’s sheer style shimmers with hand-embellished sequins, and Clio Peppiatt’s mini version adds beaded fringe for extra swing. To keep things understated, drape Markarian’s embroidered scarf or Heirlome’s silk stole over your shoulders.

Bows and bridal have always gone hand in hand, and they make for a playful hair accessory for the consummate romantic. These options from Vivienne Westwood, Completedworks, and Oscar de la Renta fit cascading curls especially well. For a subtle nod to the classic veil, go with Kamperett’s oversized piece, which trails all the way to the floor.

Trade your bouquet for blooms in your hair—or (why not!) go all out and wear both. From flower crowns to smaller clips and pins, there are endless ways to work florals into your hairstyle, especially if you consider yourself a boho bride, and picked the pastoral venue to prove it.

#6649. Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”

#6648. These Were the Breakout Red Carpet Stars of 2026

Whew—what a year it’s been for red carpets, huh? Between awards season, Fashion Month, and Vogue’s weekly celebrity roundups, there’s been plenty of statement looks to take in throughout 2026. And while there were some notable A-list standouts this year—especially those on our annual Best Dressed list—there were also plenty of emerging names who proved their status as notable rising stars.

Below, Vogue rounded up the 10 breakout stars who had especially splashy, career-making years. And better yet, these buzzy actors and singers all come armed with a unique red carpet style. Whether it’s North of North star Anna Lambe’s championing of Indigenous designers, or actor Diego Calva’s slick array of suits worn on his Club Kid press tour, these Hollywood names are making their mark with distinct fashion choices that make them stand out from the pack. (Sure, they have a team of agents and stylists—but you simply can’t buy taste.)

So, without further ado, meet Vogue’s 10 breakout red carpet stars of 2026.

North of North star Anna Lambe was busy promoting the second season of her hit Netflix series this year—and the Indigenous (Inuk) star brought a unique flavor to the red carpets, working with stylist Nadia Pizzimenti. When she wasn’t busy championing Indigenous designers such as Jamie Okuma or Lesley Hampton, you could find her slipping into sleek Louis Vuitton leather pieces—and sitting front row at the show, of course (like a true fashion It girl).

The Scottish actor gained buzz when he joined the Marvel universe this year, starring in the Disney+ series VisionQuest—but his personal style on the red carpet has been just as action-packed as the show. He and his stylist Fabio Immediato have been showcasing how cool, modern, and totally unfussy modern tailoring can be. Those tinted Prada shades at a VisionQuest screening! A fun little Valentino tie at the BAFTA Scotland Awards! Let’s hear it for a man who has fun with dressing up.

What happens when you star in one of the biggest Hollywood franchises, well, ever? Actor Whitney Peak would know: She brought some seriously epic blockbuster fashions to The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour this year. The star and her stylist Karla Welch have leaned into designs that are theatrical and extravagant—a perfect mood for promoting the film, given the Capitol in The Hunger Games is all about excess. Come for the chic Chanel gowns—stay for the Robert Wun bird dress.

Mexican actor Diego Calva may have gained attention for his role as a social worker in Club Kid, but his red carpet style is less club-rat and much more sleek, sexy and refined. He and stylist Ilaria Urbinati’s go-to formula? Injecting classic-cut suits with more unexpected details. Like his bright red Dzojchen suit and polka-dot tie, or black Loewe tuxedo with a bright-yellow shirt and tie. It’s hard to give a timeless two-piece a more irreverent personality, but Calva has it in spades.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’ve come across a dance banger by Adéla this year. (Finish the lyric: “Every single night, I pray that. . .”) The singer has had a breakout year, thanks to her hits-filled album Prima—so much so that she’s playing Coachella next year. And just as stage-worthy is her pop star approach to fashion. Working with stylist Chris Horan (a master of pop style), she’s cultivated a signature look surrounding tight corsets, mini shorts, and of course, her bright pink hair.

You may know Owen Thiele as a pro podcaster (stream “In Your Dreams”) and actor (watch Adults), but the rising star is bringing some sleek attitude to the red carpet scene. He’s been working with stylist Jared Ellner (his IRL boyfriend, fun fact), and his wardrobe for the spotlight centers around giving menswear classics a more youthful twist. Think: A suit vest worn with no shirt underneath, or a classic collared shirt with more than a few buttons unbuttoned. Fierce is fierce, honey.

It’s certainly Sienna Spiro’s year, thanks to her acclaimed debut album Visitor. The English singer won best new artist at this year’s MTV VMAs—and earned the same award nomination at the 2026 Grammys, no less. If one can describe her sound as raspy and powerful, her red carpet style can be labelled as just as soulful: She works with stylist Edie Rose to find looks that are sweet and slightly retro, pulling archival references (or full-on vintage) pieces that give her a distinctive edge.

With a commanding name like Guitarricadelafuente, the Spanish singer and actor almost has to have a bold sense of style to match. And he certainly does: The star, who is garnering early Oscar buzz for his role in this year’s La Bola Negra, has been making the press rounds in striking looks all masterminded by stylist Luca Guarini. His casual little Marni V-neck sweater at the GQ Men of the Year Awards! His sleek black Dior tuxedo at the Governor Awards! Get you a man that can do both.

When you’re playing a Disney princess like Moana, your red carpet style has to be just as enchanting—and Samoan-Australian actor Catherine Laga’aia understood this assignment fully. While promoting her live-action reboot of the beloved franchise, the actor and her stylist Alexandra Mandelkorn embraced the tropical, beachy feel of the film—with lightweight summery frocks that struck the right balance of red carpet appropriate yet utterly effortless. From the gauzy white laces to the summery polkadots, her cheery style is a breath of fresh air.

From Not Suitable for Work to season three of The White Lotus, we could simply not escape Nicholas Duvernay on our TV screens this year—not that we’re complaining about it. The star and his stylist Avo Yermagyan have subverted menswear codes to make the silhouettes and details just a touch more intriguing. A three-buttoned tan blazer from DSquared2? Check. A plaid Wooyoungmi suit with a pop-of-red shirt? Check. Serious suiting swagger? Check-check.

#6647. We Tried 6 Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies—These Are The Only 2 Worth Serving At Thanksgiving

A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

But sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That said, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

Once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”

Costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

#6646. The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in California in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he says. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”

#6645. How Did This 14-Year-Old Get Sam Bankman-Fried on the Phone?

Journalists who’ve been anxious about losing their jobs to artificial intelligence would be wise to focus on a different, altogether less menacing but equally impressive threat: 14-year-old Eli Goldfine, the shoestring podcaster from Westchester County who last week conducted a 90-minute interview with Sam Bankman-Fried, who’s currently serving a 25-year sentence in federal prison for orchestrating a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency grift.

So how, exactly, does this precocious ninth grader with braces—and not a reporter from one of the scores of legacy publications who’d surely be gunning for access to the disgraced cryptocurrency king—score an interview so coveted? “I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam’s account,” Goldfine, who hosts a podcast about prediction markets called The Supercycle, told me earlier this week. “I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case.”

Goldfine’s classmates are impressed, too, even though he’s been on the receiving end of some gentle ribbing about his on-air ad reads. But can any of them say they got Bankman-Fried to speculate on the likelihood that AI will bring about the extinction of the human race? ("Less than 50%, more than 10%," by the way). Before school’s out for Thanksgiving break, Goldfine joined GQ to talk about his media diet, dream interview subject, and the mechanics of interviewing a man behind bars.

Eli Goldfine: Wait, just to step back here. Are you printing what I'm going to say, or is this just for you to know? It's not a video on the site, right?

Okay. So my podcast is primarily about prediction markets and other broader markets. And I got into that during the 2024 election. My dad showed me Polymarket and I thought, "Wow, this is really cool. It's people staking money on different sides of an outcome. And when you put all that price signal together, it converges on a really accurate probability of a given event happening. How could I investigate this more?" So I learned more about it and I started trading on a fake-money version of Polymarket.

It's called Manifold Markets. And what's cool about that one is, anyone can create their own question rather than the platform deciding. And anyway, I got really into it and then I was like, “I'll write a couple articles about this because I have some ideas.” And then I started doing interviews and it all kind of came out from that.

I think sports betting, like FanDuel and DraftKings—this stuff obviously serves very little utility because it's just the company offering these bets to the gamblers and there's no really accurate price signal coming out of that. So does that serve such an important function? Probably not. And it's fair to say the same about prediction markets on sports. Does anyone really need to know the outcome of a sports game that badly? I mean, probably not. I don't have anything against it per se, because people spend money for entertainment on other things. I mean, this is another way to spend your money. But it's not as valuable as prediction markets in some other categories. Right?

I mean, I think I've just always had a motivation to learn more about what I'm interested in. So when I start learning about something, I just get it all in my head and then I can talk about it pretty competently, I guess. I wouldn't consider myself to have natural interviewing skill. I just think I know a lot about the things that I'm interested in.

So for news, mostly Bloomberg. For social media, mostly Twitter. And then I also read articles on Substack.

So I think I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam's Twitter account. And they said, "I run this Twitter account now, but I think you have some smart ideas about Sam. Would you be interested in taking over the Twitter account?" And I was like, "Oh, yeah, that could be fun." And my dad was like, "No, you can't do that. I don't want to get sued or anything." So we ended up talking to Sam's parents about it, and they were disappointed that I wouldn't be able to take over the Twitter account. But as an alternative, they proposed, "You should just interview Sam for your podcast." So I just thought, "Wow, that's a great idea. Let's do that."

Oh, I don't know. I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case, which we actually didn't cover very much during our podcast together, since it's already been widely covered. But, yeah, I think I just had learned a lot about the case and they were like, "Well, maybe we want someone who knows a lot about the case to be able to take over his Twitter."

I don't know. I might want to skip that one for legal reasons.

I mean, I've watched so many of his other interviews, both when he was behind bars and before that, and I feel like he talks the same way to everyone. So I'm 14, you would expect maybe the average person is going to talk a little bit differently to a 14-year-old interviewer. But for him, I think it was pretty much the same, which is kind of what I expected. He's very consistent when he's talking to different people.

So when he picked up and was like, "Hi, it's Sam," I was like, "Wow, I've heard him say this in so many other interviews, but he's talking to me. That's crazy." He also called 15 minutes before the scheduled time, so I was panicking a little bit trying to get all my questions in order and deciding what order I was going to ask them in. I mean, it was pretty intense. And also, it was split up over two days in three hour windows during each day, since he can only call for 15 minutes at a time. So that was a little bit stressful.

I mean, it's mostly what I expected. He just hadn't really gone on the record about it specifically, which is why I wanted to ask him. I think his views are pretty common. He's a part of the effective altruism community. So I wasn't so surprised when he said he thought there was a 25% chance of AI destroying humanity. Obviously, if it's the average person, that might seem a little surprising. But knowing him, I wasn't very surprised.

I think there's going to be a lot of benefit in the short term, especially when we're seeing the rate of technological progress.
