But in the long term, you have to consider that there's a few examples of less intelligent things controlling more intelligent things, and that's kind of the whole point that the doomers are trying to make. Just that, when humans were smarter than the next smartest animal, we’re the ones who dominated, right?

And mostly people just think it's funny. #6644. The 17 Best Airbnbs in Copenhagen Embrace Hygge

If you’ve spent years saving photos of Copenhagen street style and Danish living rooms, the best way to really experience Scandi fashion and design is to go straight to the source—moodboards can only take you so far. Watch locals pedal past in color-blocked coats and billowy blouses, browse the racks at Hay House, and keep tabs on how many cafés have a Louis Poulsen pendant over their counter. Winter may be cold, but it’s a great time to go and see the city in action. Tivoli Gardens lights up for Christmas and the city settles into the candlelit coziness of hygge season.

A Copenhagen apartment delivers Scandinavian style up close. Think herringbone floors, tall windows, blonde wood, and a kitchen that’s set up to actually cook in. From canal-side flats in Christianshavn to a family house a short bike ride from the center, these are the Copenhagen Airbnbs at the top of our list.

The sunny striped mural in the dining room says it all: This home has personality. This 170-square-meter apartment takes up the first floor of its building and is located in one of the oldest squares in the city, once belonging to a duke. The interiors use warm ochre tones and terrazzo tiles in both bathrooms. French balcony doors open onto a quiet inner courtyard, but for evenings and nights, the square is a cozy place to be, with candlelit restaurant windows (including one right downstairs) just around the corner.

Amenities: Fully equipped kitchen, dressing room, Wi-Fi, TV, free gym access, 24/7 support

Set in an 18th-century house on Amaliegade, a block from Amalienborg Palace, this apartment has high ceilings and old-world details like wood-paneled walls and a large hearth grounding the living room. Step outside and the Marble Church, Designmuseum Danmark, and the noon changing of the guard are just a few minutes’ walk away. If you visit during the holiday season, the Nyhavn Christmas market is just down the street.

Clean lines and a restrained palette rule in this two-bedroom apartment, located right in the middle of most of the city’s big attractions. That’s not to say it doesn’t have its quirks: Look closely, and you’ll notice more than a few duck figurines (as well as a brass pretzel hanging in the kitchen). (The fact that its surrounded by a fruit garden only amplifies its oasis-like feel.) Accented by rustic wooden furniture and a cozy fireplace, the whitewashed interiors are anything but stark.

Amenities: Wood-burning fireplace, fire pit, hammock, outdoor dining area, loungers

Somewhere between eclectic treehouse and antique treasure trove, this penthouse apartment definitely makes for a memorable stay—if only for the decor. Between the lacquered paint, bold wallpaper, and personality lighting (the fuchsia fringe lamp in the living room is of particular note), this place will soothe the maximalist traveler uninspired by Scandinavian simplicity. #6643. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6641. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

If you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

This crisp will make you forget pumpkin pie ever existed. The crunchy topping is the perfect accompaniment to the smooth pumpkin filling, creating a pumpkin dessert that is anything but boring.

Charlie Brown Thanksgiving-Inspired Chocolate Bark

#6638. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6637. GQ’s Best Gifts for Men 2026: 70+ Editor-Approved Presents

There's no shortage of stuff to buy for men. Stuff worth giving? That's another story. Fortunately, finding stuff worth giving is a salaried position around here. The results of that extensive retail research are all here: a carefully considered mix of great clothes, clever gadgets, handsome home goods, and a few things he probably wouldn't think to buy himself. We keep this guide updated throughout the year, so below you'll find our latest favorites alongside a few perennial heaters, all handpicked to make your gift-giving duties a little easier.

Still got names to cross off your list? Browse the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a steady supply of good ideas.

This Banana Republic glen plaid double-breasted jacket features a rarely seen 2x1 button stance, which makes it a touch more casual but no less handsome.

Among Ralph Lauren's many contributions to American fashion is transforming the denim shirt from a Western novelty into a staple of the modern wardrobe. This weathered slub denim version is a handsome example, and something he'll wear for years to come.

Few knits occupy a place in the menswear pantheon quite like J.Crew's rollneck sweater. With its relaxed weave and raglan sleeves, it's an enduring heater that makes for an easy gift.

What makes Morjas' Belgian loafer so irresistible to those who've had the good fortune to wear it is just how comfortable it is. Doesn't hurt that it's also clean, understated, and versatile as all get-out.

Maple's Orbit bracelet is a great little way to add a fleck of personality to an otherwise understated fit. And if this design is a little too out-there for his taste, you may have to look elsewhere entirely. That's kind of Maple's whole thing.

Smaller, thinner cases are great, and the Timex Marlin is a stone-cold minimalist classic in that world. But it also sells out, so allow us to recommend another, newer Timex gem: the Marlin Jet Titanium. He'll love that it's an automatic, too.

Patagonia's Snap-T is an icon, and this new Re-Tool Air version gives it a fresh spin with an exclusive Polartec fleece that's remarkably lightweight, wonderfully warm, and made from 100% recycled polyester.

This merino wool crewneck from Arc'teryx is lightweight, great at regulating temperature, and just as good worn on its own as it is layered under a sweater or jacket. A go-to layering piece for just about any wardrobe.

If you ask us, the Moon Shoe is one of the Swoosh's best releases of the year. A perfectly retro, low-profile runner with a refreshingly affordable price tag.

A great hoodie is essential, and Reigning Champ nails fit-meets-function better than most, with an aesthetic inspired by old-school athletic training gear. This one is cut from the brand’s signature midweight terry, which is soft and substantial without feeling bulky.

A man can never have enough flannels. Filson's Rangeland is made from brushed 5.5-ounce cotton, and we're partial to the red and gray plaid.

Massachusetts-based Steele Canvas has been making sturdy canvas goods for generations, and its Everyday Tote is exactly the sort of gift they'll most definitely get some use out of.

When we think of field watches, we think of Hamilton. This no-nonsense mechanical number is hard to beat in the category, and you could spend a lot more on a lot less.

A good pair of cowboy boots can do wonders for a fit, and Tecovas' Warren makes a strong case for adding a little yee-haw to the rotation. With classic flame stitching and a sharp cutter toe, they're more versatile than you might think.

3sixteen's asymmetrical fleece is freaky, but not too freaky, with a wide boatneck, an off-center zipper at the neck, and an oversized pocket with a zip closure. There's a lot going on, but the proportions are spot-on.

Some of the best stuff Miansai makes is low-key its bead and stone jewelry. The Avi necklace is a welcome change of pace from the usual gold and silver.

John Smedley has been making knitwear in England for more than 200 years, and there's a reason it's still considered some of the best in the biz. This wool polo might look simple, but the quality of the knit, the fit, and the finishing make it something special.

OrSlow's 105 jeans have a classic straight leg and medium rise, with the kind of easy, timeless fit that never goes out of style. A very good upgrade for anyone whose denim rotation could use a little love.

Yes, it costs a pretty penny. But it also might be one of the coolest scarves we’ve ever seen: so robust you can wrap it around yourself a few times like a sweater, at which point the price starts to make more sense. Oh, and it’s Burberry.

Movado's iconic Museum Watch has been a masterclass in minimalism since 1947, with a Bauhaus-inspired dial that's blank save for a single dot at 12 o'clock. A remarkably sleek timepiece, especially at this price.

Some days call for a full wallet, others for just the essentials. Coach's 3-in-1 gives him both, with a removable ID insert that works just as well on its own when he wants to travel a little lighter.

For the record, we're all for giving socks as presents, provided they're of the same caliber as those from Japan's Rototo.

Quince is one of our first stops for affordable cashmere, but its merino wool offerings ain't too shabby either. Take this sweater, which it done up in cable-knit for a little somethin' somethin'.

Blundstone introduced its Heritage boot this year, a decidedly more upscale take on the brand's beloved Chelsea. Handmade from premium leather, it's also finished with a Goodyear welt that allows it to be resoled for years to come.

Come for the three iconic Byredo scents, which you can spritz according to whatever the mood calls for. Stay for the handsome leather case, which is almost reason enough to gift the set on its own.

Plenty of dopp kits come in sleek leather (no shade), and plenty of designer versions cost a small fortune (some shade). But most guys just want something that looks good and can take a beating on the road. Filson knows how to do that.

Bar soaps have officially entered the elevated grooming arena, with better ingredients and better scents. Made in France, this bar adds a pop of color by the tub, lathers like a dream, and carries Frama's gorgeous Herbarium aroma that lingers on skin long after the shower.

Bleu de Chanel's Parfum takes everything great about the original and turns it up a notch. Still zesty and botanical, but with sandalwood and tonka bean lending a richer, smoother finish.

Released this year, Braun's Nevo is arguably the best and most advanced foil shaver on the market today, and our own testing backs that up. Given the price tag, it's exactly the sort of splurge that makes for a great gift.

Vitamins B and C do wonders for the skin, and Aesop's B Triple C Facial Balancing Gel is packed with both. Deeply hydrating yet leaving a matte finish, it was a game changer when it debuted over 20 years ago, and it's still elite after all these years.

If he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

The Philips OneBlade 360 is a little groomer we love for its versatility. There’s really nothing quite like it out there, and it can handle just about any hairy situation.

Dior seems to drop a new olfactory banger every few months, and Bois d'Argent is one of the latest. Smooth woods, amber, and rich iris mingle with frankincense for a scent that's warm, elegant, and easy to wear just about anywhere.

Wonder Valley's newish Wild Garden hand wash puts olive oil to good use, whipping up a rich, softening lather with a cedar-and-herb scent that brings a little of the great outdoors to the sink.

A moisturizer is a no-brainer, but a serum signals one is getting extra serious about skincare. Caldera + Lab makes that addition easy: a few pumps deliver vitamin C, collagen amino acids, and skin-soothing botanicals to brighten, firm, and soften fine lines.

We've been longtime fans of Dr. Dennis Gross's Alpha Beta Universal Daily Peel pads, which make good skincare almost embarrassingly easy. A couple of swipes help exfoliate dead skin, smooth texture, and brighten the complexion.

Tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

Salt & Stone makes one of our favorite body washes, and this mini set lets them take the whole lineup for a spin.

With these hydrating eye patches from one of the best grooming brands to do it, no one will ever know he didn't get his proper eight hours last night.

You can buy all the fancy sunscreen you want, but convenience decides if you actually wear it. Freaks of Nature’s SPF 50 stick—small, glide-on, reef safe, and water-resistant for 80 minutes—nails it.

The LED mask market is booming, and Omnilux is at the top of the heap. This one is specifically designed and FDA-cleared for men’s typically thicker facial skin, targeting fine lines, firmness, and overall health, while helping calm any redness from shaving. In other words, it’s a Michael Myers-like mask that promises scary-good skin with consistency and patience.

Hair dryers have officially gotten techy-cool, and Laifen is a big part of it. The new SE 2 is so sleek and ergonomic, with intuitive controls to match, he'll want to leave it on display.

Smythson and Burberry joining forces is more British heritage than you can wave a Union Jack at. Smythson already makes a covetable travel chess set, but add Burberry's signature check and it's, well, checkmate.

ICYMI: Menswear's patron saint Todd Snyder linked up with West Elm for a stirring collection of homewares this past year, and the hands-down standout is this walnut valet chair. A handsome place to hang tomorrow's outfit—or yesterday's, if we're being realistic.

It's a tabletop lighter shaped like a mallard duck. Something you'd find in the study of a delightfully eccentric uncle, and exactly the sort of gift no one knows they want until they get one.

A speckled enamelware thermos from Polo Country, because why not.

Few brands have done more to make everyday essentials like bedding, towels, and sleepwear into objects of desire than Copenhagen's Tekla. Its PJs embody that sensibility: beautifully cut, made from crisp organic cotton, and available in a killer assortment colors and stripes.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

If they're going to keep ordering pants off the internet, they might as well have a proper tool for opening all those packages. The Palmer knife makes short work of cardboard and packing tape, so they can get to the fit pics faster.

Hoto’s sleek PixelDrive electric screwdriver comes with 30 interchangeable bits and a nifty pixelated display that shows exactly how much power he’s working with. That wobbly dining chair doesn’t stand a chance.

It’s a well-built, thoughtfully engineered analog clock with a discreet digital display and a lovely mechanical chime. Not cheap, sure, but having one less reason to reach for my phone has been worth every penny.

It may come as a shock, but there's a whole world beyond burgers worth smashing. Caraway's immaculately designed grill press is up to the task.

A good set of bedsheets is a nice gift. An adult gift. It says, “I care about you, even when you're unconscious.” Parachute's brushed cotton sheets are those sheets: soft, cozy, and something they'll appreciate every single night.

Shinola's Michigan-made five-port power supply is a highly specific gift for the design obsessive in your life, but that's precisely why it'll hit.

Few things feel better than slipping into a plush robe at a fancy hotel, but honestly, most have nothing on Brooklinen's. Better yet, you don't need to spend $500 a night to get one.

#6635. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6631. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6629. How Women Weavers Are Preserving Indigenous Amazigh Culture in Morocco

Malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains. The 36-year-old weaving artisan is enjoying a glass of milk and a plump, juicy date from a large plate she’s set out for guests—myself among them—when she looks up to see even more people arriving. To accommodate the new visitors, she finishes her milk, leaves the room, and returns with a low table. Then another. And another after that.

Soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven. Malika shifts the tables around to make room for the additional food, and her brother, Mohammed, rearranges the pillows that line the rug-filled floors of the space. It continues like this for the next couple of hours: A table appears here, a pillow moves there. Food comes in and food goes out. The only thing that stays put? The rugs themselves.

Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal. In Morocco, Friday is celebrated as "Couscous Day," a cherished tradition where families gather for a communal lunch, usually after the weekly congregational prayer.

“In a typical rural Moroccan household, everything is mobile except the rugs,” Jihane Lahbibi, the Moroccan co-founder of the Moroccan rug brand Casa Amar, tells me as we dunk our Tafarnout into the tagine juices. “The pillows, tables, mattresses…they are all roving. But the rugs are the constant. Symbolically, they are the pillars. They anchor the room. They are the room.” In fact, as Malika echoes later through a translator, rugs are the most sacred part of the home. “When you welcome guests,” she says, “the rug is everything.”

Malika was the first weaver Jihane and her Italian husband Matteo met when they began looking for artisans to make custom rugs for Casa Amar back in 2021. Today, they partner with women in five communities across Morocco to create and source rugs for clients across the world, and were even part of Milan Design Week last year. As interest in Moroccan craftsmanship and design continues to soar, I’ve come to spend some time with a few of the artisans Jihane and Matteo work with to learn more about the Amazigh weaving culture behind the craft.

This scene with the roving tables is a very good start. It’s impossible to miss the deep significance of rugs in everyday Moroccan life once you experience their starring role in every room, after all. But as the days go by, I realize rugs have taken on even more meaning in recent decades, too: They’ve become a way to keep Amazigh culture alive in the face of modernization.

“Younger generations aren’t making as many rugs these days, so when the older women weavers eventually die, the younger ones won’t know how to make them—and that makes me really, really sad,” Malika tells me after we’ve finished our tagine and have moved on to mint tea and a bowl of grapes for dessert. “So now, when I’m weaving, I think about my culture. I also think about the satisfaction of making something good, and the money I will get from making it. All of those things are important. But rugs are objects that last, and because they last, they are one of the best ways to preserve the culture.”

Like most Indigenous traditions around the world, Moroccan rug weaving dates back thousands of years. Amazigh women (also known as Berber) in the Atlas Mountains originally crafted handknotted rugs from local sheep’s wool to protect themselves and their families from the elements: harsh sun during the day, and freezing mountain temperatures at night. Over time, rug weaving morphed into an art form as well, one filled with all sorts of storytelling and symbolism. Some rug patterns represent universal emotions like love and hope, while others are more like talismans, meant to protect against evil and infertility. No matter the pattern, though, the weaving tradition itself has never been written down anywhere. It’s passed down from mother to daughter simply by watching.

Nejma Oubzou prepares freshly harvested dwarf palm by cutting the thorns off and separating the fan-like leaves in order to dry them out. The fibers are used to create woven items such as baskets, mats, and home decor.

“Amazigh women know how to make rugs the same way many other people around the world know how to make bread…it’s just a part of the culture from a very young age,” Jihane, who grew up in Casablanca, tells me one afternoon as we’re driving through the mountains. “It’s not like someone sits you down on the loom and says, ‘This is how you do it.’ It’s just that you learn the same way you learn how to walk: No one tells you, you just learn it by seeing.” When she started Casa Amar in 2021 after leaving her job as a business lawyer, she used to ask the artisans she met when, exactly, they learned to weave for the first time. But now she’s come to understand that seeking out that information was always a fool’s errand. “I realize now that it was never so specific,” she reflects. “It was always: They’re around, they see, and they try.”

That’s exactly what happened with Malika. She wove her first rug at age 15 after years of watching her mom weave, and then watching her weave some more. But that first rug she ultimately created wasn’t just a result of growing up around looms; it was a way for her to care for her own mind. When she was 10, her older brother asked her to drop out of school. Their sister had just gotten married, their parents worked outside the home in agriculture, and he and his younger brother wanted to stay in school—so he decided Malika would be the one to stay home and handle the household chores. Weaving became her creative outlet as a result. “What happened was that after I finished my household work, I had this emptiness that I wanted to fill, and weaving was how I filled it,” she tells me. “I didn’t go to school and I didn’t work, so weaving was how I took care of my brain. I used it to fill a void.”

Today, Malika continues to weave to fulfill her creative dreams, and to make money by doing so. She works independently in the home, not as part of one of the thousands of weaving cooperatives scattered throughout Morocco. When she’s weaving a custom rug for Casa Amar, she follows the design given to her by their clients. But when she’s weaving just for herself or her family (which is increasingly rare due to her growing amount of paid work), her patterns are instinctive and intuitive, usually based on how she is feeling in the moment. “There’s no particular reasoning behind so many of my designs; it’s just what I like and what my mind tells me to do,” she explains. “It’s a very free process. It’s not like if you have green, you have to put yellow. You can do whatever you want. It’s all in the mind when you’re making a rug for yourself.”

But aside from earning a living and expressing her creativity, there’s a third reason Malika weaves: a desire to preserve her craft in the face of modernization. This is where things get slightly complicated because, in some ways, the tradition is thriving. As any design aficionado knows, the allure of Moroccan textiles is increasingly global and well-documented, everywhere from Instagram to the pages of this very magazine. According to the international research firm 6W, the Moroccan rug market is projected to reach $485 million in the US by 2032, up from $371 million in 2025.

Every step of the wool preparation process is done by hand. After the wool is sheared from the animal, the artisans wash, brush, and spin it into yarn.

New York-based interior designer Sarah Lederman believes this uptick in interest could be a response to, take a guess, AI. “People are craving more handmade items in their homes now because they’re the opposite of uniform,” she says, “and Moroccan rugs bear the mark of the person who made them.” They’re a reminder, in other words, of what it means to be human.

Khadija Rhandouss in the carpet section of the weekly souk in Khmisset. Rhandouss is a local businesswoman who trades in Moroccan rugs. Every Tuesday she attends the weekly souk in Khmisset where all the best rug deals happen before sunrise.

At the same time, there are threats to the longevity of traditional rugmaking. For one thing, as Malika mentioned at multiple points throughout my visit, fewer young women are actually learning the traditional weaving techniques required to make said rugs. The work is time-consuming, after all, and the money isn’t always great. And now that there are more profitable career options available elsewhere, many younger women are choosing to leave their villages in the mountains, making weaving less of an obvious path than it once was.

Nejma Oubzou spins wool into yarn at her home in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.

That’s not to mention the modern technology that has changed the game even more. In the early 2000s, some Moroccan small producers started to buy machines from China that allowed them to process bad-quality wool (known locally as “dead wool”) to make carpets. While starting a new rug used to begin with cutting pure wool from sheep, these machines—which are still used by many today—make it easy to cut out that step entirely. This eliminates a huge and significant part of the process. “A lot of people think that making a carpet is just about weaving on a loom, but actually, making the raw material—i.e., transforming it from sheep to the wool that allows you to start weaving—is just as important,” Ibrahim Noubl, a longtime Moroccan rug dealer, told me in Marrakech at the beginning of my trip. He owns Soufny Art Gallery on the edge of the medina, and often collaborates with the beloved, art-filled hotel El Fenn just a two-minute walk down the road. “In Morocco, we are very sentimental people. We believe in lots of non-material ideas, like the thought that wool is blessed,” he explained. “When blessed wool is inside your home, it will bring you comfort and joy—but all of that disappears when it’s not alive in the first place.”

Mimouna Fadil attaches the wool to a wooden plank to start a new rug at her home in Khmisset.

Artisans, particularly from the Amazigh communities, hand-dye the wool using traditional techniques, often boiling it with ingredients to create long-lasting, eco-friendly colors. Red wool in Moroccan rug making is traditionally achieved using natural dyes derived from plants, minerals, and insects to produce vibrant, lasting colors. Earthy reds often come from henna or madder root, while brighter shades are created with pomegranate peels or cochineal insects.

With that in mind, vintage rugs are one of the best bets for high-quality wool, Ibrahim advises, because the product has already survived a few decades—so you know the wool is good. (Carpets made from “dead wool” often start to smell after a few years.) But to keep the ancient traditions alive in a competitive marketplace, companies like Casa Amar, Salam Hello, and the ever-popular Beni Rugs also sell new rugs and put traditional, sustainable craftsmanship front and center. Not only do they use high-grade natural wool (no “dead wool” to be found here), but they also work directly with artisans like Malika, helping provide an income that allows them to continue their traditional and beloved craft.

Nejma Oubzou, mother of Malika, in her bedroom in her home in the Atlas Mountains. Her name means “stars.”

Many of the artisans even pray before they sit down at the loom because it’s such a sacred act. They start with the Arabic phrase “Bismillah,” which means “in the name of God,” then follow it up with a prayer for peace and serenity during their time on the loom, often including phrases like nsaliw l mensej f salam ou l hna: “We started with peace; may we finish with peace.” After all, as Jihane tells me at various points over the course of our week together, a rug can be both sacred and a source of income. The two are not mutually exclusive. “To buyers, rugs may be just random objects, but people pray before making them, even for people they don’t know,” she says one Friday over Friday couscous, a longtime weekly tradition in Morocco. “I never want to romanticize weaving, because at the end of the day, artisans make the rugs to survive. But both can be true. Just because you have to earn money doesn’t mean you don’t make it respectfully the way your elders did it. It’s something you do with dignity and pride…something to carry the legacy.”

For the last leg of my Morocco trip, Jihane takes me to Khemisset, a small market town about an hour’s drive inland from the capital Rabat, where she lives with Matteo and their two (adorable) young sons. Khemisset is known for its surrounding countryside—think rolling wheat fields, fragrant eucalyptus trees, and grazing sheep—plus its Amazigh weaving traditions, particularly its regionally specific palm mats. Not many artisans make these mats anymore except those in the Khemisset countryside and a few others scattered throughout the Atlas Mountains, and they are sadly going extinct as a result—so I wanted to see them before it’s too late. Jihane and Matteo are also trying to help preserve the mats by spreading the word to their customers. “It’s simple: If people know about them and buy them, artisans will keep making them,” she tells me in the car on the drive from Rabat.

Unlike handknotted rugs, these palm mats are woven from dried palm leaves (not wool) and embroidered with colorful wool patterns on top. They typically cost much less than wool rugs because the raw material is cheaper, but they’re equally difficult to make—and a bit harder on the hands. The leaves tend to dry out during the day, even after the artisans boil them for softness and place them in sachets. As a result, the six women I meet—all of whom collaborate with Jihane and Matteo—often weave late into the night when it’s cooler, or in the morning before the sun becomes too strong. Despite these challenging conditions, they love what they do and are determined to keep the craft alive. (Not entirely unrelated, they are also determined to stuff me and Jihane with more dates, milk, Tafarnout bread, olive oil, and honey—the welcome spread of choice throughout our journey.)

Nora Rhandouss, Khadija Rhandouss, and Jihane share mint tea in Khadija’s salon in Khmisset.

“The techniques to make these mats are very old and very ancestral,” 60-year-old Fatiha Amalou, one of the artisans, tells me as we snack on a bowl of particularly glistening dates. We are sitting on a green and white patterned rug on the floor of another artisan’s house, where we’ve all gathered to chat. Not surprisingly, we’re also circled around a low table that, wouldn’t you know, magically appeared when we arrived. “The mats are so sacred that back in the old days, when people would die, we would wrap them up in them to take them away for burial,” Fatiha continues. “They were like a cape.”

Today, she is dedicated to preserving that sacred weaving tradition. But she also cares deeply about the craftsmanship itself. “Of course I want the legacy to continue; everyone wants the legacy to continue,” she tells me. “But really, perhaps more than anything else, I want to make something that makes me proud. We always say: If you make a good thing, it means you have a good head.” Another artisan, 51-year-old Khadija Rhandouss, nods in agreement. “When I make something good, I feel at peace,” she says. I tell them all that, as a bit of a perfectionist myself, I can relate to that sentiment wholeheartedly. Fatiha just laughs and smiles. “Yes, weaving is what we need to do to make money,” she says, “but it’s also part of what we do to feel good. It’s part of who we are.”
