#6619. Ballerina Farm Is Opening a Restaurant, Farm Store, and Cooking School—Here’s a First Look

It’s a glorious late-September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me. A soft breeze hints at the seasonal shift that will soon blanket this bucolic corner of Utah in frost. I’m standing beside two of Daniel Neeleman’s daughters and Daniel himself, his head full of curly hair and his feet tucked into work boots. He exudes the easy familiarity of an old friend, despite a family name—and now a social media presence, thanks to Ballerina Farm’s 20 million–plus combined followers—that has taken on a life of its own.

Still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me. “We love small agriculture and the diversification of it,” he says. “I think that we can make an impact in helping people see that small agriculture can work. Whether you’re doing an agritourism aspect or not, we still think it should and can be profitable.”

He speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America. Daniel did not grow up with animals and still remembers how mesmerized he was the first time he saw a cow. “I tell people on the farm tours all the time, if your endorphins are going off watching these animals, watch out. You might be a farmer. It doesn’t go away—it might come back to you later in life.” From the very day that Daniel and his now famous wife, Hannah, bought their first farm in 2017, he knew this was where they were meant to be.

Earlier that morning, I was sitting at their kitchen dining table over a brunch of quiche, greens, yogurt, and tea made from just-picked mint, the spread illuminated by beeswax spindle candles. “It’s our responsibility, and our love and passion too, to build this,” Hannah tells me, wearing a white dress with three daughters by her side. She’s sitting against a backdrop that’s become familiar to millions who have watched her cook and feed her growing family on a farm less than an hour outside Salt Lake City.

Despite their sincere intentions, the Neelemans’ endeavor has brought moments of global controversy. The internet has scrutinized their approach to homeschooling their nine children, their family wealth, and how they balance their roles as parents and cofounders. “We don’t take the platform that we’ve been given lightly,” Hannah says. Agriculture, she explains, has been at the heart of the project from the beginning, even as its reach has expanded far beyond the Kamas Valley. “It has worn a lot of different hats as it’s grown. We were young city kids, and we craved something real and knowing where our food comes from.”

Now, what began as a story told online is becoming a universe people can actually step into. On a stretch of land that spreads out beyond the window like something from “America the Beautiful,” they’re planning—and here announcing—one of the country’s most ambitious new farm hospitality destinations: a cookery school, farm-to-table restaurant, farm store, and spaces for agricultural education and events, all set within a working farm encompassing livestock, organic gardens, a dairy, and a forthcoming creamery.

At the heart of the vision is a cookery school, scheduled to open in 2029, that is as much about learning to cook from the farm as it is about taking those lessons home. The goal is to teach people how to cook seasonally and adapt when certain ingredients aren’t available, wherever they might live. (Daniel describes this as an education in life skills rather than formal chef training.) “I want students to have time with the dairy, the market garden, the creamery, so they’re seeing where the food comes from,” Hannah notes.

The cookery school will be guided by a philosophy similar to that of the legendary Ballymaloe Cookery School, where Hannah and Daniel spent 12 weeks in 2025—and first met Michael “Tiffin” Griffin, a beloved longtime instructor who has since joined Ballerina Farm as the director of the culinary experience. (A more formal, fine-dining restaurant may eventually complement the school.)

But visitors can step into the new Ballerina Farm world as soon as fall 2027, when a Dutch barn is slated to open at the site of the current Kamas market. Inside will be a restaurant and café, which the couple collectively calls an “eatery,” serving meals featuring the meat, dairy, and produce grown on the surrounding farm—a considerable expansion of the current menus at the Midway store and food truck.

Across a breezeway, a market will offer fresh produce straight from the garden and meat and dairy from the livestock—think onions, pea shoots, beets, rib-eye steaks, smoked paprika goat cheese, and gallons of A2/A2 cream-top whole milk—as well as a growing selection of prepared sides, sauces, and meals, from pickled torpedo onions to just-juiced turmeric ginger shots to chicken salad. The latter is Hannah’s particular favorite. “We got so attached to the chicken salad that we had this summer, because we grew meat chickens. We harvested them. And they made the most delicious chicken salad. Then Tiffin told us this week, ‘One more week of the chicken salad—I’m out of pickles. You’ll see it next spring.’ And I went, ‘Nooo.’” She laughs. “I think people are getting back to how grandma used to cook. She cooked from the garden, and it was amazing food.”

Just-cut spinach and radishes will sit next to Ballerina Farm’s signature products, initially available only online, as well as Ballerina Farm’s home goods like oven mitts, aprons, and wooden measuring spoons, with the name appearing only discreetly. They also launched their first skin-care product just this month: Tallow Tin body butter—made with tallow from the cattle, naturally.

The restaurant, farm store, and connecting courtyard will be more than five times the size of the existing Ballerina Farm store and café that opened in 2025, 25 minutes down the road in Midway. “There’s an awful lot of hullabaloo about Hannah doing it, but for me that’s what I saw when I was a kid,” Tiffin, the culinary director, tells me. “That’s how my grandmother lived her life.”

Over a two-hour meal of Ballerina Farm roasted chicken, garden carrots, pickled onions, and homemade yogurt, I sat enraptured by Tiffin’s story and the depth of knowledge and experience that had brought him to this particular farm in Utah. While guests can expect a diversity of dishes—Tiffin is especially passionate about Moroccan flavors—the land is the final decision maker. “We’ll ask Tiffin what’s on the menu for an event,” Daniel explains, “and the first thing he’ll say is, ‘Let me call Madison [Goodman], the head grower.’”

Goodman is responsible for a vegetable operation that will eventually expand to five acres. The kitchen will draw on its harvest but supplement it with neighboring producers when necessary—a philosophy similar to that which guided Tiffin at Ballymaloe: “If we can’t grow it, we get it locally. If we can’t get it locally, we’ll get the best.”

The design and architecture of the project, meanwhile, will be led by Patrick Williams of Berdoulat, the British design house known for its richly textured, historically informed interiors. At Berdoulat, the mantra is “the house rules.” But as Williams puts it, “In this instance, where the buildings are yet to exist, the land rules.” His designs draw inspiration from 19th-century settlers’ homes and agricultural buildings in the Kamas Valley (and, yes, the family’s famous farmstead).

The Ballerina Farm team has worked closely with Kamas officials for years now to define what can be developed on its 14-acre property, prompting the city to introduce new agritourism zoning in 2024. The plans also protect the property’s conserved wetlands. “We are constantly in touch with the city,” says Brad Roberts, the brand’s director of marketing. If done well, Kamas can become a role model for the many other small towns grappling with their own decisions around the opportunities made possible through agritourism.

Yet the Kamas Valley is not the most obvious place to craft such an ambitious project that’s certain to draw travelers not only from the coasts but also from overseas. (Eighty percent of Ballerina Farm’s 10 million–plus Instagram following is based outside of the US.) A high water table can flood the gardens, frosts set in as early as October, and voles relentlessly try to work their way into the harvest. But the valley has a certain quality of light, giant skies, and an openness that feels rarer than ever in today’s world.

Walking through three high tunnels filled to the brim with produce, I eventually met Goodman, a fourth-generation farmer who ran his own successful community-supported agriculture program in the Kamas Valley and was courted for years by the Neelemans before joining the Ballerina Farm team. He speaks passionately about the farm’s recently earned USDA organic certification and the decades of advocacy that brought those standards into existence. “You can make me cry, because there are a lot of people who fought hard for this,” Goodman says, describing the certification’s baseline standards as the floor while emphasizing that he’s reaching for the ceiling. “The label helps us bridge this gap that we, as a society, have created between our reality.”

He continues: “Everything here has a story. I can tell you the story of the winter leek. I can tell you the story of these girls.” (The girls are chickens.) He then spends 10 minutes explaining to me exactly why these chickens—Freedom Rangers rather than the more commonly raised Cornish Cross—are so special and how they’re raised from chicks to harvest. “It’s hard for me to do this and not believe in a creator,” Goodman says.

One of the challenges and opportunities of an agritourism project is that, in a four-season destination like Utah, the experience will be remarkably different depending on when visitors arrive: tomatoes in the summer, spinach in the winter, chicks in one season, and a mature flock in another. “There’s something beautiful about eating what’s in season and retraining us as eaters to appreciate that,” Hannah reflects. “I have started to notice that I’m craving spinach, pumpkin, and squash because your body wants the things that are growing.”

The culture side of agriculture has probably played a larger role in the Neelemans’ agricultural pursuits than they expected, however. While Hannah started sharing on social media as a way to kick-start business for their nascent pork operation, it snowballed into a public inquisition over what many perceived as an idealized, regressive performance of rural domesticity. But what the public wanted to know most was how it was possible. What was real? And who funded it?

When I ask them about balancing their ambitious vision with the realities of building a farm and business, Hannah says, “That’s a true founder of a company. They are the one who has to hold those two worlds together. We have to keep the dreams alive and the fire burning, but we’re also camping over the farm stand or dealing with broken pipes and trying to put up hoop houses.”

Daniel adds: “We’re the ones that decide whenever there’s money left over at the end of the month from the business.” He says that every individual part of the business is profitable. “We don’t have any investors, we don’t have any partners—it’s just us. So then it’s just a question of, What projects are we going to conquer first? We are a for-profit company, and we have to be good stewards of the finances of all the things. It has to be sustainable.”

For years, people have been asking to visit, Hannah explains, sending her messages asking to meet the animals, help with chores, or simply spend a day on the farm. At the time, the Neelemans weren’t equipped to receive this audience of millions who had developed a relationship with a place they’d never visited. Now, they’re preparing to welcome both admirers and curious outsiders, as well as farmers and cooks, into the world that has generated so much conversation. “We have a community that wants to be a part of it,” Hannah recalls thinking. “So how do we build it?”

This new expression of Ballerina Farm places Hannah and Daniel among a lineage of visionaries in farm hospitality who have transformed working farms into gathering places—Ballymaloe, yes, but also Daylesford Organic in the English Cotswolds and Babylonstoren in South Africa. But of course, one important factor sets Ballerina Farm’s journey apart. Rather than building a hospitality destination and then finding an audience, the Neelemans are working the other way around. The relationship is already shaped by years of watching the family’s life unfold online—and by the very different ideas people have formed about what Ballerina Farm represents.

It’s easy to understand the appeal: Rather than watch a 60-second video on their phones, visitors can pull sourdough or slip on a Ballerina Farm oven mitt and slide a pork chop out of the oven. They can greet a just-born calf. Their children can run the fields, breathe the fresh Utah air, and taste the milk from Daniel’s cows. As I pulled through the gates of Ballerina Farm in my rental car and watched six Sebastopol geese waddle in front of me, even I felt that very modern feeling of disorienting familiarity upon experiencing a person or a place in the flesh that I had only ever seen on a screen.

Right now, the Kamas property has already begun hosting farm dinners, seasonal events, and agricultural experiences alongside the market and food truck. Each offering showcases how the Ballerina Farm world will eventually come together: market, meals, events, education, animals, and gardens all in one place.

And for all the ambition of what Hannah and Daniel are building, the idea at its heart remains deeply personal. “The greatest work that we can do is in our homes and our own families and our communities,” Hannah tells me, a conviction that has remained constant even as Ballerina Farm’s audience has rapidly grown.

Adds Daniel, “We’ve accomplished some things that we’re proud of, but we’re far from being done.”

#6618. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6617. Ina Garten Makes A Pretty Convincing Case For Thanksgiving Over Christmas

The Barefoot Contessa knows exactly what she wants out of a holiday.

Christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just showed up with string beans.”

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

"Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

It makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

#6614. Veruschka, the Shape-Shifting Supermodel Who Defined an Era, Has Died at 87

Richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty. She could be imperious or impish, feral or feline, androgynous or opulently feminine. She could contort her impossibly long limbs into unreal configurations, traversing fashion magazines and the wider public’s consciousness with ease in a way that had never been done before. One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion’s great performance artists.

On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.

It was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, issue. Across those pages, Veruschka leapt and pirouetted, her hair fashioned into a long, swinging braid by hairstylist Ara Gallant. Avedon had found in Veruschka a woman who could give physical expression to his imagination and whose own imagination was every bit as expansive. Here was a woman whose beauty “demands something, and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever,” said Avedon.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia), Veruschka’s early life was marked by the horrors of war. She was five years old when her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed for his involvement in the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. The family was imprisoned by the Nazi regime, and the aristocratic world into which she had been born had all but disappeared by the time the war came to an end.

An art student, she was discovered in Florence in 1959. Her early forays into modeling were not immediately fruitful: Standing over six feet tall, she was an unconventional proposition even then. An initial stint in New York proved disappointing, but in Italy she developed a fruitful creative relationship with photographer Johnny Moncada. Some 3,000 images from those formative years, undiscovered for decades, would eventually form the basis of the book From Vera to Veruschka: The Unseen Photographs by Johnny Moncada and an accompanying exhibition at London’s Somerset House in 2014.

Her greatest act of reinvention was, arguably, the creation of Veruschka herself. Adopting the Russian-sounding diminutive of her first name, she cultivated a persona of indeterminate provenance and mystique. Returning to New York in 1964, she found an industry increasingly receptive to her brand of beauty. In Diana Vreeland, then editor in chief of Vogue, she found a kindred spirit.

The 1960s heralded the ascendance of a new breed of model, with the likes of Jean Shrimpton, Twiggy, Donyale Luna, and Penelope Tree becoming cultural figures in their own right. Veruschka, with her high forehead, sculptural cheekbones, and elongated limbs, was one of the decade’s most arresting presences, whatever aesthetic she took on. She appeared on 13 American Vogue covers, working with the likes of Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst, and David Bailey, and became one of the highest-paid models of her generation.

Some of her most enduring images were made in collaboration with the Italian photographer Franco Rubartelli, her creative and romantic partner. Among them was the indelible 1968 photograph of Veruschka in Yves Saint Laurent’s lace-up safari jacket for French Vogue, an image that distilled the designer’s new vocabulary of female sensuality and authority.

Veruschka was also an endlessly inventive beauty muse. The Vogue archives are rich with examples of her aesthetic adventurism. She sports fantastical lashes, intricately braided hair, graphic eye makeup, and elaborate headpieces. She was chameleonic, which made her popular with the hair and makeup artists of the era.

And her fame extended well beyond the pages of fashion magazines. In Michelangelo Antonioni’s seminal 1966 film Blow-Up, set in Swinging London, Veruschka played a version of herself in a brief but electrifying scene opposite David Hemmings’s fashion photographer. A year later, she graced the cover of Life magazine. Few models before her had so thoroughly captured the imagination of the wider public, and her legacy lives on in the new generation of celebrity models today.

By the mid-1970s, however, Veruschka had grown disenchanted with the fashion industry. Her artistic ambitions began to take greater precedence over her modeling career. In collaboration with the German artist Holger Trülzsch, she embarked on a captivating body of photographic work in which her painted figure dissolved into architectural surfaces and natural environments, or assumed entirely different identities.

In 1971 Veruschka also appeared in West German magazine Stern with 27 other women under the coverline: “Wir haben abgetrieben!” (“We’ve had abortions!”) to advocate for abortion law reform at a time when it was illegal. It was a significant moment in Germany’s ’70s feminist wave.

Still, fashion never entirely relinquished its fascination with her, nor she with it. There were occasional returns to the runway, including for Chanel in 1994 and, at the age of 71, for Giles Deacon’s spring 2011 show in London. In 2017, Acne Studios enlisted her for its resort 2018 look book. In contemporary photos—with her silver hair slicked back, sporting oversized, louche tailoring—she looks every bit as modern as she had half a century earlier.

Veruschka on the red carpet at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015.

Much has been made of Veruschka’s otherworldliness, but there was something profoundly human in her commitment to metamorphosis. At the height of her fame, she could have made a career out of being the most beautiful woman in the world. How much more interesting, instead, to become a thousand different women.

#6613. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6612. 17 Best Beard Trimmer Picks, Tested by GQ Editors in 2026

Every guy needs the best beard trimmer for his situation. Whether he grows it patchy, keeps it perma-stubbled, or is as lustrous as the A-List beards, a trimmer is mandatory in every beard kit. And not all beard trimmers are alike, which is why the best one for your facial hair style may be different from the next guy’s.

I tested a bunch of beard trimmers to deliver you a real who’s who of men’s grooming devices. This list reflects a range of options—some multitaskers, some detailers; some top-shelf, some a better buy for lower budgets. Above all, though, I ask you this: Make sure that the device you choose allows your beard to reach its full potential. That doesn’t mean you need a big bushy beard, but rather, you should be able to achieve whichever style (or a suite of styles) you want to wear over the next few years—which is the minimum amount of time any of these devices should last. Ideally, they’ll hum on for five to 10 years, anyhow.

Here are the best beard trimmers after we tested pretty much every last one of them. (And while you’re at it, consider my rosters of other grooming tools, from razors and electric shavers, to manscapers and hair clippers.)

No sense in burying the headline: Philips Norelco’s Multigroom 9000 Series is, hands down, the best beard trimmer you can buy. And that’s before factoring in how much more it can do than just keep your facial hair in check than other electric razors that are found in your everyday grooming kit. (It’s also recently been renamed the “All-in-One 9000” but answers to both names.) For the last 5 or 6 years, this has been my single go-to trimmer. Everything else is trying to dethrone it, and so far, no true contest has emerged. In terms of customization and power, this device checks all of the boxes.

It all starts with the beating heart: "The Multigroom does not compromise on power or battery life, and it's very intuitive to use," says Fellow Barber’s Head of Education Emily Clark. The battery life truly over-delivers: your mileage may vary since Philips Norelco only claims a (still impressive) six hours of charge, but I got a ridiculous 17 hours of consecutive runtime fresh out of the box, thanks to a lithium ion battery. Speaking of the box, there’s a lot in there, all of it useful. Between the small tooth-like detail attachment and foil shaving head, the Multigroom 9000 makes it easy to style and sculpt with precision. One trimmer even adjusts by tenths of a millimeter to help you get the perfect designer stubble, if that's your aim. And that’s just its beard trimming bona fides. The Multigroom 9000 is also a solid hair trimmer (shout out to that brawny motor and battery again) and body hair trimmer as well. Covering off for three products, and doing it well, suddenly makes the $90 price tag look like a deal.

Long-term testing notes: Wouldn’t you know it… I lost the beloved little shaver on this one recently. Heartbreak. (Yeah, I can test a new one, but I realize now how much of my love for it is pinned on that micro shaving attachment.) I stand by the fact that it’s the best on the market, but without that shaver, the window has opened for me to spend time with other devices, like the Braun below. Let this be a lesson: Don’t unpack your Philips Norelco all-in-one in a hotel room without carefully auditing every single piece when you pack it up again. Adam Hurly

"This trimmer is great! It comes with so many attachments to use for your trimming needs. The battery lasts a long time, i have yet to have to charge mine and i've had it for a few months now.

The trimmer is super quiet as well as very well made. It's all made up of metal, not plastic, and feels like it will last a long time. It's fairly lightweight and easy to handle when [using] it. It also comes with a small cleaning brush that makes cleaning it up a breeze!"

Given how much I love the Philips Norelco Multigroom 9000, it’s no surprise that the more affordable model, the Multigroom 5000, is my budget choice to keep things manscaped. It offers most of the same steel-bladed precision and customization benefits as its fancier family member, albeit in a less durable body (plastic instead of stainless steel) and half the battery life. Still, its a three-hour battery power beast that bests many beard trimmers twice the price. And the lighter plastic body is nice for travel. The Philips Norelco Multigroom 5000 is great for anyone on a budget, but it’s not “budget."

Whereas other lower-priced beard trimmers can’t handle precise detailing, the Multigroom 5000 includes a detail trimmer and nose trimmer, not to mention hair clipper and body trimmer guards for versatility. It does lack the shaving detailer and the body shaver (as does the in-between 7000 model), which is important to note if you want that level of customization and don’t otherwise own a detail shaver that you also rely upon for bare-faced stretches of facial real estate. For this reason, I find it a little less perfect across the board compared to the 9000, but the price-to-precision ratio is hard to match. And if you want a great value above all—and a straightforward beard trimmer—meet your optimal Multigroom, the 5000.

Long-term testing notes: Recently, I used the 5000 consistently, and got quite cozy with it. Sure, it lacked the key shaving features of the 9000, but I think this is truly the best value device in the game when you only want a trimmer. Terrific muscle, terrific customization, great endurance. Five stars for this one. Adam Hurly

"This Phillips/Norelco trimmer works great. It is very quiet, the battery life is pretty long and it does exactly what I need it to do. It comes with a lot of attachments - haven’t used them all, but the ones I have used worked just fine. This is a good quality trimmer."

Hatteker is a surprise of a buy—it’s that “out of left field” Amazon brand that most of us recognize by name, despite not knowing anyone who uses it. This all-in-one kit covers every kind of hair-trimming task, from lineups to sideburns to beards, eyebrows, and body hair. What's more, it's a hair-cutting machine for full beards and stubble alike with multiple plastic guards. I bought the tool with little expectations for quality and care, but was consistently surprised at how well it held its own compared to the more reputable brands.

This device won’t win any design awards and certainly hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but most consumers won’t care about that stuff; they want a good beard trimmer that meets all their grooming needs, and Hatteker’s checks all of those boxes. I do wish its detailing trimmer was a bit narrower, but that’s me minding some very fine details. It’s also not up to the same quality as, say, Philips, Andis, Braun, Wahl, etc, but it’s also not low quality either. For $40, you get your money’s worth, especially considering that LED battery display and vast range of trimming lengths and clipping attachments. It’s still a great option if you’re not looking to spend a lot, or if our other best value winner, the Philips Norelco Multigroom 5000 Series, is out of stock.

Long-term testing notes: Every time I bring this one out, I am amused by how surprisingly great it is. It goes to show that those Amazon reviews really are one of the most accurate depictions of value; I long wrote the brand off because of its non-image compared to the big names, but in terms of performance and return on spend, Hatteker really clears the bar. Granted, I’m not using most of these devices more than a few times a quarter (since by and large I stick with my own favorites or test new ones) but my Hatteker remains strong and sturdy and has endurance, some three years after I first acquired it. Adam Hurly

"The trimmer is easy to use and the charge lasts a very long time. I have not had to recharge since the initial charge after taking it out of the box, trimming bi-weekly. It is not heavy. It’s easy to handle. The adjustment guides stay where you select. I don’t worry about them shifting during use. Beard maintenance is an easy job with this.”

The All-in-One 7000 makes a convincing case for clearing some space in your bathroom cabinet. A body hair trimmer that comes replete with several beard-related attachments, its precision comb kept stubble neatly between 1-3mm without pulling or leaving stray hairs behind. Sure, a dedicated beard trimmer will do a more precise job, but there's plenty of substance to this device's delirious accessory count.

The slightly boxy handle feels reassuringly secure when I'm cleaving away at a couple of days' growth, while a textured grip makes it well-suited to comfortably swerving across my chest, underarms, and more sensitive areas. If you dig them out from the bottom of their box, the nose and ear attachments prove useful enough to earn their place in the kit too. Philips rates this kit for up to five hours between charges – handy given how often you'll be using the thing – and the waterproof construction makes cleanup straightforward.

My main gripe is one that always crops up when I test Philips, Braun, and other established grooming brands’ devices – the proprietary charging connection. You’ll need its supplied cable, even if your drawer is already overflowing with USB-C leads. Still, for someone who wants to maintain short facial hair and keep the rest of their grooming in order with one tool, the 7000 covers a lot of ground. Esat Dedezade

“It's comfortable and quiet with an easy-to-adjust head that's great for both beard and mustache maintenance. The precision comb is handy for controlling length too, and there's very little tugging around the neck. And if you leave it a little too long to get your beard into shape? It holds its charge surprisingly well when tucked away in a bathroom cabinet.”

Like the Philips Norelco Multigroom models, Braun's All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 is a jack-of-all-trades option that can do far more than tidy up your beard; the box is packed with a nose and ear trimmer, a precision head, and longer guards, too. But what separates this trimmer from the rest of the pack is the built-in dial that offers 40 trim-length settings. It’s top-notch precision in minimalist packaging. I think it’s the only real contender for the top spot on this list—perhaps that price and slightly less enduring battery are its shortcomings compared to the Philips Norelco 9000, but I do find it a superior device in terms of ease and design.

Where other devices require you to swap out different heads or attachments, or ask you to pick between bigger length gaps than you’d prefer, Braun’s Series 9 offers half-millimeter increments from 0.5 to 20 without having to futz with extra accessories. In my testing, that made the trimmer the most user-friendly device on this list—no swapping guards as you fade your beard or neckline. Plus, the Series 9 is fully waterproof for those of you shaving-in-the-shower fans looking to speedrun your morning regimen. (And I’ll admit, shaving in the shower certainly makes clean-up—of both the beard hair mess and the trimmer—faster and easier.) Bottom line, Braun’s All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 is exactly what the name promises. If it seems a little expensive, that’s because a beard trimmer that can handle all these tasks, and handle them well, isn’t cheap.

Long-term testing notes: As I said above, this one has been getting lots more mileage from me lately, and I am so pleased with that fact. I absolutely adore how easy it is to navigate between the smallest minutiae of trimming lengths without swapping guard heads, and that detail shaver has been so clutch at keeping my neckline, cheeks, and beard perimeter cleaned up. My one complaint from a recent trip was that it’s quite difficult to repack everything into the carrying case, if you bring along all attachment heads. Besides that… perfect grooming tool. Adam Hurly

“Before this trimmer came into my life, I made a couple of cheap purchases. The style I like it's 1mm overall with a 2mm on my chin and 2.5 on my mustache. The problem was the other trimmers could not handle it on a daily basis. I am the type of guy whose beard grows back really fast, so I'd trim my beard. Then, the next day, you could see clear growth, and when I tried to do it again, it just wouldn't trim the same. I'd end up hurting my face a little bit. Not this trimmer. This trimmer can handle my beard on a daily basis without hurting my face. It's that good and efficient. It's built for heavy performance and durability. For the first time I am able to maintain my beard on a daily basis.”

Wahl is a pedigreed name in the professional and home grooming worlds, but that doesn’t mean it’s done innovating. Its new High Visibility trimmer has a killer app: the trimming attachment is angled so the teeth sit “above” the base, letting you get eyes on the action in the mirror as you mow through facial hair. It’s maybe not a priority if you’re just doing leisurely trims, but if you’re trying to get the perfect line at your cheek, sideburns, or neck, that little bit of offset is a godsend.

Suddenly I’m seeing very clearly exactly where the blade is hitting. If you’ve ever had to drop that cheek line too far down or do the back-and-forth thing with your burns, you’ll recognize what a game changer this is. The Wahl High Visibility trimmer’s laser-pointer precision is boosted by some of the best ergonomics in the game. The body’s relatively thin with an excellent rubber grip, which lets you hit difficult angles like a professional pool player. The High Visibility trimmer is new to the market, but I’m betting it’ll become a barber favorite—and yours, too, if you’re doing daily touch-ups to keep those lines looking sharp.

Long-term testing notes: I find myself using this more often as a detail trimmer than a full-on trimmer. I think it’s a fantastic trimmer through and through, but I pull it from the bullpen as a closer; that’s where I hold it mostly in my mind—and happily! Adam Hurly

"Absolutely amazing product. Heavy, rock-solid construction makes the hand feel confident, has great ergonomics, and has a solid grip even when the hand is soapy. But the best part is the forever blade makes it easy to see what’s getting cut, even with guard on (I used the 2). Most precise edge for a jawbone line beard I’ve ever had. And with the guard, it combs as it cuts with the grain of the hair, keeping stray whiskers knocked down. I’ve been pinched/cut before with fatter spaced blade rakes, but I didn’t feel threatened trimming under the nose."

The MultiShape lets you build a grooming kit around the things you actually use. Start with this beard and hair trimmer, then add a nose trimmer, foil shaver, or even a toothbrush head if you want them. Everything shares one rechargeable handle, which makes much more sense than finding room for another charger every time you buy a new device. Other manufacturers – take note.

This starter kit includes the lithium-ion base, beard and hair head, and two combs. The other attachments cost extra, so factor those in before deciding how much money or luggage space it’ll save. Panasonic rates the battery for 90 minutes, with a one-hour charge.

Long-term testing notes: Over several weeks, I used a broader MultiShape kit for shaving, beard maintenance, and brushing his teeth. Swapping heads was quick, and the light handle made the shared system easy to live with. The beard head coped with ordinary growth, although particularly stubborn hair exposed its limits. With daily toothbrushing and shaving three or four times a week, he charged the handle roughly every fortnight. That convenience made it a favorite for travel, while a dedicated beard trimmer remained the stronger choice for dense growth. Owen Gough

"The upside of buying a beard trimmer that can double-up as an electric toothbrush with the right attachment is you've got one tool to rule them all. The challenge? You might need a couple of passes with the trimming head to get an even finish. Compared with the more traditional alternative, it's a bulkier device with its guard fitted.”

For anyone whose morning routine involves keeping a few days’ growth under control, the dedicated Beard Trimmer 7000 keeps things pleasingly straightforward. Its adjustment dial covers 40 lengths, while the textured handle gives you something secure to hold before the first coffee has kicked in.

The dial is the main reason to choose this over a kit with a bag of fixed guards. You can adjust the length without hunting for the next comb, then use the detailing attachment to tidy the edges. It’s a more focused choice than Philips’ all-in-one kits if beard maintenance is the job you actually need done. Just don’t mistake the hair collector for a return of the old vacuum trimmer – it’s another part to empty and clean.

Long-term testing notes: I found the Series 7000 easygoing around my chin and sideburns, with little cleanup needed for stray hairs. Its reassuring weight and textured grip also helps, even if the plastic finish isn't quite on par with Philips' now-retired all-metal Series 9000. Truthfully, this trimmer did struggle a little around the awkward patch beneath my nostrils with its bulky combs making it harder to get a neat finish. I also don't bother much with the removable hair collector – I'd rather clean the sink once rather than wash another attachment. As an everyday trimmer, this is still a solid pick. Rob Leedham

“This trimmer is perfectly functional for its price, and its two-hour battery life means I'm yet to be caught short without any charge mid-shave. As much as I appreciate its efficiency, I do miss how the older metal design looked on my bathroom sink-top. This plastic iteration feels cheap (and a little flimsy) in comparison.”

No attachments; no problem. For a beard trimmer that can only do one thing (but is damn good at doing that), Manscaped's Beard Hedger will make light work out of the bushiest, burliest beards. Its zoom wheel controller lets you dial in the comb's length between .5 and 10 millimeters for even shaves, while the waterproof construction means you can shower and shave to save time on your morning or nighttime rituals. The built-in comb is great for picking up hairs that are stuck to your face so that every strand gets whacked, because few things are more unsightly than stray long hairs poking out from an otherwise well-groomed beard. Adam Hurly

“I've owned maybe 5 or 6 beard trimmers over the last 15 years. Make no mistake, this is the most expensive, but hands down it's also the best (that includes competition from Braun, Philips Norelco and Wahl). The quality is the first thing you notice as soon as you unbox it - the feel of the handle and the quality of the blade, even down to the USB charging cable which doesn't have the usual cheapness you'd expect from an accessory that's something of an afterthought.”

If you’re researching beard trimmers, you’ll see the term “zero-gap” a lot. So, what’s a zero-gap trimmer? A zero-gap trimmer cuts as close to the skin as possible, effectively a 0mm cutting length. That can make them dangerous for novices, as you can easily cut your skin or ears while you trim. But for the highest possible level of precision, that’s what you want. (The Bevel Trimmer can also be adjusted so it has a slightly longer taper.)

This trimmer was designed by Black men, for Black men, and damn does it look good. It’s a work of art that design lovers will appreciate. This sculptural device will look mighty impressive on your bathroom counter and feels phenomenal in your hand. It’s a true barber-quality trimmer, perfect for guys with curly or Afro-textured hair. It’s also one of the most powerful trimmers for home use, with a 6,000 RPM motor. Despite that, it beats all comers in terms of battery life, with an 8-hour charge that will last for months. A word of warning: This trimmer doesn’t come with any attachments or comb guards. That’s by design, as it’s a precision trimmer for making clean lines and shaping up longer beards. If you want to cut precise hair lengths, opt for the Bevel Trimmer Pro or purchase extra attachments like the T-Blade. Adam Hurly

"I’ve been cutting my own hair for years. Let me tell you these are the best trimmers I’ve ever used. Nothing on the market compares. I mean every word. The best!!!! Switch the original blade that comes with it out with the t-blade and I promise you that line up gone be crispy like bacon! Bevel with T-Blade is King!!!"

One more Philips Norelco device, for good measure and good reason: This tool is adored by both our expert source and me: I love the OneBlade for its ability to switch between trimmer, shaver, T-blade, and body groomer with aplomb. I think it's one of the best-designed tools in facial hair care right now, and a dozen other brands are releasing dupes to chase the same high.

“I appreciate how affordable it is and how easy it is to find at drugstores since so many clients ask me where to buy it because they love it too,” says DeZarate. “There was one week where I needed to buy three of the OneBlade for different clients during press events, so that they were able to actually travel home with it because they loved how easy it is to use and that it's universal. It does a really nice job at creating clean lines and is great for sensitive skin.” This one is easy to torque in different directions, too, allowing its shaving function to act like a T-blade trimmer while also offering familiar cartridge-shave movement for anyone who wants an entirely clean mug or simple a neckline tidy up. Get one with the body grooming attachment, too, and you could have an all-in-one grooming device for all facial and manscaping needs; it really does it all with that one singular blade.

Long-term testing notes: Like DeZarate, I frequently reach for this guy to mind the details; it’s an easy tag-along for any trips (especially if I need some body trimming all the while) and will certainly be with me on a big three-month trip I have to take soon; it’s a terrific head-to-toe customizer, though I don’t necessarily rely on it when I’m at home and have dedicated devices for each task. It is a terrific middle-ground pick, for the guy who wants things streamlined. Adam Hurly

“I have to admit, I’ve avoided this product for the past few years. For some reason I didn’t think it was something I needed. I recently started maintaining my beard on my own more and needed something with a bit more precision. Safety razors and straight razors were cutting up my face. My $200 electric razor cuts good, but is terrible at getting straight edges. So I figured I would give this a try and I must say I’m very happy with it. This is a very high quality product for the price. Not only does this razor provide the precision I needed to line up my beard, but it also shaves very very well.”

Vacuum trimmers keep you from having dozens of errant clippings littering the sink, but this one is more than just a vacuum—it has a detailing and edgework attachment and can trim up to 18 mm with a line-drawing detail head that rivals most T-blade trimmers.

Panasonic's wet/dry beard trimmer has a convenient wheel that lets you switch between guard lengths effortlessly—a huge boon when you're trying to shape your beard.

A display screen on your beard trimmer? In this economy? If it seems too good to be true, we get it, but this easy-adjusting trimmer from Panasonic is, in fact, the real deal.

For just 25 bucks, you can get this all-in-one trimmer from Philips that does a surprisingly good job when it comes to shaping and maintaining your scruff. Is it the fanciest trimmer on the list? No, but it works.

You want a beard trimmer that’s simple, effective, and doesn’t come with useless features or add-ons. Here are a few features to consider when looking for a great beard trimmer.

We look at how evenly a trimmer cuts, how comfortable it is to use, and whether its attachments make different jobs easier. Power matters, but so do the small frustrations that become obvious with regular use – awkward combs, difficult cleanup, or a handle that’s hard to hold. We also compare battery life, charging, and the range of cutting lengths against the price.

Adam Hurly has reviewed grooming products since 2013, and his years of testing underpin this guide. Timothy Beck Werth contributes his own hands-on findings alongside his wider coverage of grooming and consumer technology. For this update, we’ve also drawn on my reviews for British GQ, with the relevant tester and any differences between British and US kits identified in the entries. Read more about GQ and how we test and review products.

There’s no denying: The Philips Norelco Multigroom 9000 is the best beard trimmer you can buy these days. If its $100 price tag is too steep, the baby-brother Multigroom 5000 is a solid fallback. It’s not shower-proof, has a shorter warranty (five years to the 9000’s eight years), has a plastic body instead of steel, and comes with a few less attachments. But at $40, it gets the basics done nearly as well as it’s pricier sibling.

Can you use a beard trimmer to cut head hair?

Beard trimmers are not meant to be used as hair clippers, since clippers require much more power to cut through thicker patches of hair. However, some beard trimmers have the muscle to multitask, and they’ll proudly hype that skill—usually by declaring the work for “beard and head” or similar language. We usually verify those claims against product reviews, too. And frankly, we’d probably just opt to buy a dedicated hair trimmer (you can find our roundup of the best hair trimmers here), especially if you’ll be using it often.

Barbers choose tools to suit the job, from adjustable trimmers for controlling length, to detail trimmers for sharper edges. The Wahl Pro Series High Visibility is our professional pick for precision work, while the Philips Norelco Multigroom range offers broader versatility. For home use, start with your beard length and the kind of maintenance you do most often – a tool built for crisp outlines won’t necessarily include the guards you need to trim a longer beard evenly.

Which trimmer number is best for a beard?

That's going to depend on what beard style you're going with. In order to play around with trimmer numbers, we like the Braun All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 9440 for its easy-to-use adjustment wheel.

First, wash and dry your beard so you're starting off with a clean canvas. Then, decide how short or long you want to keep that bad boy. Trim against the grain of your growth, and know that the direction of growth may vary even in similar locations on the face. It's OK to make a couple of passes to ensure you get each hair because a patchy beard is a bad beard. Finally, clean up the neckline with some sharp lines so it's neat and tidy, framing the perfection that is your beautiful facial hair.

How do I maintain and clean a beard trimmer?

Switch it off and disconnect the charger before cleaning, then remove trapped hair from the blades and combs after each use. Follow the instructions for your particular model – a washable cutting head doesn’t mean the whole handle can go under the tap. The Remington Vacuum trimmer, for example, has removable washable parts, but its body should stay out of water.

Let washed components dry before putting them away. Oil the blades if the manufacturer tells you to, but don’t assume every trimmer needs it. Philips’ current Multigroom blades are designed to work without oiling. Replace a damaged or persistently blunt cutting unit with the correct part for your model.

How do I choose the right trimmer if I have sensitive skin or ingrown hairs?

Avoid “zero-gap” trimmers, which is a trimmer that cuts as close to the skin as possible, effectively a 0mm cutting length—those can mess your skin if you're prone to irritation or ingrowns. Otherwise, since you're trimming, you usually won't have to worry about irritating your skin because the blades shouldn't ever actually make contact with your face.

What’s the best way to travel with a beard trimmer—any TSA or voltage concerns?

One of the big concerns for frequent travelers—at least in the USA—is whether they're going to be able to get their beard trimmer through security and not having it buzz during transport. If this is a priority for you, look for a model with a travel lock like the Braun All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 9440, which prevents the trimmer from turning on in transit.

How do I clean a waterproof vs. non-waterproof trimmer?

Waterproof trimmers are a breeze: Just hit ‘em with the (usually included) cleaning brush, then wash them off in the sink before drying and applying some oil. Non-waterproof trimmers just skip the rinse, so you’ll have to take extra care with the brush. You can also use spray cleaners specifically designed for grooming electricals depending on your trimmer's care instructions.

What should I do if my trimmer starts pulling hair or losing power?

First, make sure you've thoroughly cleaned the trimmer. Next, make sure it's fully charged and/or has new batteries. If it's still pulling hair, it's probably time to swap the blades (plenty of companies sell refills on their site, and make sure to check the warranty to see if you qualify for a fresh set). If it's losing power, it might be time to swap the internal battery (check your warranty!) or get a new trimmer altogether. Luckily, we haven't had that issue with any of the trimmers listed above.

Emily Clark is Head of Education at Fellow Barber and a Senior Barber at Fellow’s SoHo NYC barbershop.

Melissa DeZarate is a celebrity groomer whose clients include Matt Damon, Kenan Thompson, Matt Bomer, and Taika Waititi.

#6611. The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

The simplest Thanksgiving side deserves better.

In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so important. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

In the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a big batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

#6610. Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor

With a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6609. Every Time Veruschka Was on the Cover of American Vogue

Veruschka, the legendary German model who helped revolutionize fashion photography during the late 1960s and early ’70s, has died at the age of 87, a family member confirmed to the German newspaper Bild.

The statuesque beauty was known for her collaborations with the leading photographers of her day—Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, and Bert Stern among them—and many of her most enduring shoots were originally published within the pages of Vogue. It was the magazine’s visionary editor in chief Diana Vreeland who famously championed the six-foot-one newcomer after discovering her in Paris and urging her to drop her aristocratic surname, recognizing her as a perfect conduit for the era’s psychedelic, boundary-pushing spirit.

As a result, she appeared on the cover of the magazine some 12 times. In the year of 1965 alone, she was a Vogue cover star on five separate occasions. Seen together, they serve as a remarkable document of fashion’s seismic shifts throughout the 1960s, her endless versatility as a model, and the remarkable alchemy she shared with many of the era’s most extraordinary image makers.

Here, see every time that Veruschka was on the cover of American Vogue.

#6608. IHOP Is Bringing Its First-Ever Collectible Coffee Mug To Restaurants This Holiday Season

It’s getting increasingly difficult to keep up with all the limited-edition tumblers, advent calendars, and seasonal releases that disappear off shelves before you’ve finished your morning coffee. And now IHOP is giving breakfast lovers another reason to make room in their kitchen cabinets.

Delish can exclusively reveal that IHOP is launching its first-ever Collector's Holiday Mug on Monday, November 30, with the mugs being sold at participating restaurants nationwide. It’s also the very first time the pancake chain has ventured into selling merchandise directly to customers—and, as it turns out, the idea has been brewing for quite some time.

According to Samantha Strong, IHOP’s executive director of brand calendar strategy, the company has heard from enough coffee-loving customers over the years to realize there was an actual appetite for owning an IHOP mug. “What started as a frequent question has grown into a genuine fan obsession,” she said, and this holiday release is now the company's first attempt to turn that enthusiasm into something people can actually buy.

IHOP says coffee is its second best-selling menu item, which means an awful lot of people have spent their mornings clutching one of those mugs while waiting for breakfast. But before you start planning an entire IHOP-themed kitchen makeover, know that each participating location will have just 24 (yes, only 24!) mugs available. Once they're gone, they’re gone, at least as far as this limited-time release is concerned.

There's certainly no shortage of things to collect this holiday season, but at least this one’s something you can actually put to use while doing some damage to a stack of pancakes.

#6607. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6606. 12 Huckberry Gifts for Guys Who May or May Not Own a Cabin

There’s a guy on every gift list who dresses like he lives off the land, even though the land he lives off is mostly takeout. He’s got the waxed jacket, the wool socks, and a thermos he treats like a family heirloom. He’s never had to use any of it in an emergency, but if the moment ever comes, he’ll be the best-dressed guy in the woods.

Lucky for you, Huckberry was made exactly for this guy. I went on a full expedition for gifts that are tough enough for the real thing and good-looking enough to wear every day: a ballistic nylon Filson briefcase, Japanese selvedge denim, elk leather Hestra gloves, and even a Jeff Goldblum perfume that smells like a campfire in the best way. It’s gear with real craftsmanship behind it, the kind he’ll reach for constantly. Will he ever actually need any of it? Unclear. Will he look great not needing it? Absolutely.

He’ll be ready for the wilderness at a moment’s notice, even if the wilderness hasn’t called yet. Until it does, pick any of these and you’re covered, no camping required.

Made from ballistic nylon, which is a fancy way of saying it can take a beating. The bridle leather handles keep it handsome enough for a meeting, all while being tough enough to survive getting tossed in the back of a truck he doesn’t own.

The official footwear of the guy whose favorite trail runs from the couch to the fridge. Cozy enough to lounge in all weekend and good-looking enough that he’ll “accidentally” wear them to get the mail.

For the guy who insists vinyl just sounds warmer, despite not having the tech to prove it. The built-in preamp means it plugs straight into speakers, so there’s no excuse not to finally play that record he bought for the cover.

Yes, it's a Jeff Goldblum fragrance, and yes, it's actually great. Brain Dead's collab opens with sandalwood, tobacco leaf, and leather, so it smells like a campfire at a very nice lodge. He'll get compliments, and he'll credit Jeff.

Every guy deserves a proper cup for a post-hike pour, and this earthy little vessel from Danny D's Mud Shop has way more charm than a plastic shot glass. Use it for whiskey, espresso, or whatever he's toasting with.

Japanese selvedge with all the rugged good looks and none of the miserable, stiff-as-cardboard break-in period. Ideal for a man of action, or at least a man who looks great standing next to a campfire.

The kind of sweater that looks like it was passed down from a grandfather who really knew how to chop wood. The two-tone brown and black knit goes with everything from denim to cords, and it'll only get better with every passing winter.

Barbour has been dressing guys for the countryside for over a century, and this quilted jacket is the easiest way in. It's light enough to layer under a heavier coat or wear solo on crisp days, and the sage green is outdoorsy without being too literal.

Hamilton made watches for soldiers in the field, so this one is technically military-grade, even if his toughest mission is brunch. It’s hand-wound, which means he gets a small, satisfying daily ritual and a great excuse to say “my mechanical watch” out loud.

Hestra has been making gloves in Sweden since the 1930s, so it knows a thing or two about cold. These pair soft elk leather with a fleece lining: warm enough for a snowy hike, sleek enough that he won't look headed for the slopes.

Rototo is a Japanese knitwear brand, and this scarf has the kind of craftsmanship you can feel. The lightweight wool-cotton blend keeps him warm without the itch or the bulk, so he can wear it from first frost straight through to spring. It also has a little artisanal cred, which he’ll absolutely bring up when someone compliments it.

RRL is Ralph Lauren’s love letter to rugged Americana, and this plaid workshirt is the most convincing ranch hand costume money can buy. It’s built like the real thing and looks broken in on day one, ready for chopping wood or, more realistically, a Saturday at the bar.

#6605. Sheet-Pan Cider Vinegar Chicken

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

Scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.
