#6604. Veruschka: The Late ’60s Supermodel’s Best Beauty Looks of All Time

There are few faces more synonymous with the youthquake of the ’60s than Veruschka, who has sadly passed away at the age of 87.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort in East Prussia, the German countess was discovered at 20 years old while studying art in Florence. Soon after, she decamped to New York City, where she changed her name from Vera to Veruschka and became one of the most—if not the most—in-demand supermodels of the decade, regularly appearing in the pages of Vogue and lensed by greats such as David Bailey, Irving Penn, and Richard Avedon.

Standing six feet tall, she was a bombshell with a chiseled-by-the-gods bone structure, steely blue gaze, plush mouth, and shape-shifting champagne-blonde hair. Her “indomitable career of beauty,” as Susan Sontag once famously deemed it, was characterized by portraits of her sinewy silhouette, immortalized most notoriously in that scene from Michelangelo Antonioni’s cult 1966 film Blow-Up, where she poses for photographer David Hemmings’s camera to amorous effect.

As for her countless evocative close-ups, which showcased her otherworldly hair and makeup looks, nothing was too decorative or directional for Veruschka, and it was this perpetual gameness that made her a favorite of Diana Vreeland during her tenure at Vogue. There were her sculptural, teased-to-the-heavens, and decidedly ’60s hair looks, from a voluminous bouffant with waist-grazing lengths, to an origami-like knot, to the tornado of face-framing braids that she wore in a 1967 editorial shot by her longtime lover and collaborator Franco Rubartelli. And then there were her signature extreme lashes, which ran the gamut from classic, doll-like fringe to cast in Technicolor shades or granddaddy longlegs lengths, and were often punctuated by a sheer wash of pastel pigment on the lids, graphic winged liner, and glossy pink lips.

“The most beautiful woman in the world,” according to Avedon, and a true chameleon in every sense of the word, Veruschka’s metamorphic fluency continues to be a lethal and enduring combination in the fashion world. In fact, in 2017, Acne Studios tapped Veruschka to star in its Resort 2018 look book, where she wore the collection’s cropped jackets and slouchy trousers with a sharp slick back and statuesque swagger. Here, a look at her most striking beauty looks of all time.

#6602. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6600. 6 Products That Changed My Life in November—And Would Make Good Gifts

Chances are you are reading this while awash in the joyful glow of an active oven and/or open laptop chock full of Black Friday sales. As someone who can’t help but enjoy America’s annual week of consumption, I have some advice: You can probably skip that fourth slice of pie and also, when it comes to gift-giving, bigger is not always better. Personally, some of the best presents I’ve received over the years are small but meaningful items that come with a sense of personal connection and discovery: A set of irresistible Japanese incense from an aspirational boutique my fiancé found in Tokyo’s Aoyama district. Some adorable silk painted ornaments that my mom stumbled upon at a local maker’s market. Employee merch from NASA, where my stepfather worked. All that to say, the ritual of gift-giving is always made to be much more meaningful when we can collect all the little, delightful items we’ve collected over the year and share them with those whom will appreciate them most. Maybe that’s a simple, but utterly practical thingamajig that has made your life that much more convenient. Or something you came across in your travels. Even an item you have at home for years that you couldn’t imagine living without. Here are a few self-care accessories that I've encountered both recently and not-so-recently that fit that bill.

Ever since the days of chewable Flintstones vitamins, we as a human race have been striving for new, inventive ways to get our daily dose in. Straight pills are boring and require water. Powders are messy and not easily transported. Gummies can be overly sugary and harden over time. But strips are nearly weightless, easy to travel with, and consumable on their own. The ones made by StripIt dissolve on your tongue, a little like a Listerine mint strip, and come in four different formulas: Vitamin C, D3 + K2, B12, Sleep, and Digest. Though they can take a little bit longer than a mint strip to dissolve, they’re still a really convenient way to make sure you’re keeping up with your supplements. I’ve been using the D3 + K2 ones while I travel. They taste pretty good and are colorful and novel enough to function as a small stocking stuffer or Hanukkah gift for the health hawk in your life.

I will never tire of a big, beautiful block of soap. Especially if it's so fragrant that it fills a whole room with its smell. My new favorite in this category is Life Research Lab, an herb-forward brand that takes inspiration from (and incorporates) the local LA flora into its soap blends. There’s the eucalyptus and grapefruit pumice slab that draws from common neighborhood trees, a classic “cowboy cologne” mix of cypress and California sagebrush so commonly found in Angelenos’ gardens, and a juniper bergamot number that lifts scents from the desert. Many of them contain bits and pieces of the very plants they’re named for, which function as light exfoliants as you scrub. I was especially charmed by the Christmas Morning Soap, which is infused with balsam fir essential oil and pinyon pine leaf. Its name, price, and the fact that it comes in both 9-ounce blocks and 4-ounce cylinders make it a perfect stocking stuffer. T’is the season.

When I traveled to Seoul a few years ago, I popped into the Hinok store and spent about 20 minutes smelling basically every one of its products, which all contain ingredients sourced by foraging detritus from old cypress forests on Jeju island (not cutting them down). Alas, I couldn’t bring anything home because my carry-on was already stuffed. But recently I learned the brand is available to buy in the US and had a chance to try a few things out. My favorite is the thick, gooey body wash. It has the consistency of honey, and emanates a light, fresh natural scent without being too overpowering. Most crucially, the formula is gentle enough to clean your body without stripping it of its natural oils. After searching for a light body wash I can use daily for a while now, this qucikly became my new favorite. (The deodorising spray is really good for households with pets too.)

When I was in New York last month, my future sister in-law suggested we take a quick field trip to Senti Senti, a little skincare store in Chinatown. To my delight, they carried imported Korean and Japanese formulas of lotions, cleansers, and—most importantly—sunscreen from popular brands like Beauty of Joseon and Bioré. (Don’t ask me how this is allowed, Chinatown’s gonna Chinatown.) In the 15 minutes we spent there, we observed at least three people walk in and beeline for this Dr. Althea face lotion and I couldn’t help but be tempted. Using it for the past month, I’ve been impressed with how light, hydrating, and easily absorbing it is—an excellent goop to apply in the morning. For anyone who hates the lingering feeling of a heavy day cream, this one’s a no-brainer.

We’re days away from the start of winter, meaning we’ll all be heating up our homes and braving, windy, sub-zero temperatures more regularly for the next few months. All of that means our skin has a far higher chance of getting dry and flaky. Enter Bein All-Over Body Oil. The blend of organic sesame seed, squalane, and camellia oil rubs on smoothly and absorbs like a dream, leaving no sticky residue behind. Body oil can be especially helpful for feet, knees, elbows, and hands, post-shower. And is light enough that you can apply lotion on afterward, too. Best of all, the San Diego-brand’s products smell faintly of bitter citrus, like a little Aperol spritz for your skin. It’s bright-red packaging makes it feel especially festive for the holidays.

A good robe, in my humble opinion, must rise to a few crucial tasks. It should be able to absorb water well, dry out quickly, and let your skin breathe after a long warm soak in the bath or shower. It should also allow you to lounge around your household without flashing your living companions or getting furniture wet. That’s why I’m partial to a long linen kimono, which checks all of those boxes. I was gifted a sophisticated blue-striped one from Deiji Studios nearly six years ago for Christmas, and it’s now a perfectly worn-in, indispensable bathroom staple. No wonder Deiji still sells it. Even better, it’s on sale for Black Friday.

#6599. People Are Calling The Day Before Thanksgiving ‘Green Wednesday’—And It’s Becoming A Huge Holiday

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting roasted.

Thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

If you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly announces they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery company Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence company BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

According to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The company’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok users sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

As Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those users, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

Americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an important reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

#6598. Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too quickly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in our August 2023 issue and has been updated with additional guidance. Head this way for more of our favorite pecan recipes →

#6597. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6596. Can Your Home Boost Your Endorphins? 7 Simple Tips for a Healthier, Happier Living Space

On a recent cold Sunday morning, I had no interest in doing anything except hiding from the world. Then I did a few small tasks that completely shifted my mood. First, I spritzed a home fragrance with notes of orange and cinnamon around my apartment; next, I raised the blinds to let in some sunlight and tidied up the living room—clearing away clutter, folding blankets, and fluffing the pillows on the couch. As I did, I recalled the words of Loewe’s perfumer, Nuria Cruelles, about one of her candles: “It has the power to transform your house into a home.” That’s exactly what I was doing, simply by adding a bit of scent and straightening up. Another expert, Dr. Rodrigo Arteaga, explains that anyone can turn their home into a “place that improves their health” by following a few simple habits.

There are indeed many small routines we can adopt to turn our home—the place where we relax and let our guard down—into an environment that fosters well-being. Psychologist María Martínez echoes this, encouraging people to practice the Japanese philosophy of kaizen, which emphasizes the transformative power of making gradual, continuous improvements to our lives. “It’s important to create an environment where you look around and like what you see,” she says. “This releases endorphins and makes you feel good. If instead, everywhere you look, there’s a reminder of a task you need to do, something unattractive, or clutter that causes stress, you’ll end up feeling worse. If it gets bad enough, you’ll soon stop wanting to be in your own home. You’ll find reasons to leave or stay late at the office, coming home only to sleep. These are all signs that you need to make changes—not just in your life, but in your home, which should serve as a sanctuary where you can recharge.”

Here are seven practical tips to help create a home environment that helps boost your mental and physical health.

When Florence Pugh was asked in a recent Vogue interview what a perfect day off looks like for her, one of the first things she mentioned was buying flowers. “I love going to my florist and putting together a beautiful bouquet; it makes me so happy,” she said. She’s not alone. According to a study by Dr. Nancy Etcoff of Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, flowers ward off worry, anxiety, and sadness. Study participants felt noticeably better after having flowers in their homes for just a few days—and tended to place them in the kitchen, dining room, and living room, the spaces where they spent most of their time.

Whenever possible, open your curtains and blinds in the morning. As Dr. Arteaga points out, “This gives your brain a powerful signal to synchronize its biological clock. Natural light helps your body recognize when it’s day and when it’s night, giving you more energy during the daytime and helping you rest better at night.” After dusk, create “light islands” inspired by the Danish philosophy of hygge, which offers plenty of ideas for designing a wellness-focused home. As Meik Wiking explains in his book My Hygge Home, you can bring warmth to dark corners of a living room using lamps that cast light downward and bulbs that emit a soft, warm glow. Floor or table lamps placed near a sofa or reading chair work especially well. For more general lighting in spaces meant for relaxation, hygge experts recommend ceiling or wall fixtures with glass or fabric shades that diffuse light gently, rather than harsh overhead chandeliers or pendants.

Studies show that listening to music you love provides an immediate boost to your well-being. “Music has an instant, almost magical effect on us,” explains psychologist Marta Calderero. “Within just a few seconds of hearing a favorite song, your brain is flooded with endorphins and oxytocin. That’s why you suddenly feel that rush of euphoria and such an intimate connection to a track. And it doesn’t stop there—after a couple of minutes, the brain begins releasing dopamine, making us enjoy each second a little more than the last. It’s the most beautiful way I know to regulate emotions and reconnect with the present moment.”

Hygge inspired another recommendation on our list. As Wiking explains, styling a small corner of your home with cozy lighting, blankets (a hygge staple), pillows, a plush rug, and a few favorite objects creates a dedicated spot to unplug from the world. It’s a simple way to build an inviting nook that signals to your brain that you’re in a safe space where it’s okay to relax and unwind.

Going barefoot indoors is another of Dr. Arteaga’s recommendations, and Beatriz Crespo, an expert in healthy micro-habits, seconds the idea. Beyond its physical perks—like improved circulation and balance—walking barefoot reduces stress and encourages relaxation through direct contact between the ground and the nerve-rich soles of your feet.

Proper ventilation offers clear microbiological benefits, as biologist María Dolores Cima Cabal explains: “It helps reduce the density of microorganisms that accumulate inside the home.” At the same time, it delivers real psychological perks, since breathing fresh air reenergizes the body and supplies oxygen to the brain. A Harvard University study confirms that cognitive function can suffer—and reaction times slow down—in stuffy environments.

Returning to that chilly Sunday morning at the start of this piece, candles have a unique ability to turn a house into a home through the evocative power of scent. When you choose an appealing fragrance—whether as a room spray or a candle—your brain registers it as a cue that you’re somewhere you can let your guard down. “Smell is the sense that most powerfully triggers memories, and the one our brain responds to with the greatest intensity,” concludes Calderero. “It forms a direct link between a scent and an emotion. If you keep a signature scent at home, that olfactory connection becomes so strong that the moment you smell it, your brain associates it with rest, comfort, and warmth. Choosing a specific fragrance helps your brain recognize that it’s in a space where it doesn’t need to stay on high alert—and your nervous system naturally slows down.”

#6595. The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Launched in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

Much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Launched in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

When I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

Imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Launched in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere new—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

This was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Launched in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Launched in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Launched in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Launched in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

Alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being quickly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. Serve it with crunchy crostini or pita chips at your next dinner party, and your guests will go crazy.

#6593. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6592. The Maldon Salt Scandal, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.)

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a new study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its big flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

#6591. Still, No One Does Thanksgiving Style Quite Like 'Gossip Girl’s' Blair Waldorf

With my sincerest apologies to Vogue staffers’ favorite pairs of eating pants, when it comes to Thanksgiving fashion, nothing beats the fresh-off-the-runway and fabulous pieces found in Gossip Girl’s now-legendary Thanksgiving episodes. When there’s a svelte Fendi suit or a tapestry McQueen dress on hand, who needs a forgiving drawstring waistband?

Nearly twenty years after the show’s debut, the finer details of those episodes’ familial dramas may be a little murky in memory, but nothing remains as crystal clear as Blair Waldorf’s sharply-defined, uptown girl style. See, for example, the sparkly fall 2007 Marc by Marc Jacobs babydoll dress she dons in season one (episode nine, “Blair Waldorf Must Pie!”). “It’s a defining look for both the character and the show, and I have spent the better part of two decades trying to duplicate it,” says People Like You author and Gossip Girl fashion expert Tyler McCall. “And if you don’t believe that it’s iconic, try and find that dress on the secondhand market for anything close to a reasonable price.”

Blair Waldorf-approved Marc by Marc Jacobs dresses may not have quite reached the CBK-Calvin Klein craze, but do a cursory search, and that particular babydoll dress is still incredibly difficult to procure. But when paired with a knit capelet, bow-printed tights, and a dainty pair of pumps—as it was in the episode—Miss Waldorf’s holiday style could be easily mistaken for the secondhand wishlist of many fashion girls today.

Season 6: Fendi suit, Gucci blouse, Chloé overcoat.

Another treasured Thanksgiving look of Blair’s includes season two’s backless green dress from the now-shuttered label Alexandra Vidal, topped off by a blue Sretsis dress (worn as a coat!) and some seriously autumnal Jimmy Choo boots. However, when it comes to rivaling the babydoll dress, it’s season three’s Nanette Lepore belted tweed coat, worn over a brown printed Sariah dress, and—once again—statement tights that handily take second place. Today, thanks to Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, not-your-mother’s tweed is all the rage.

While vintage fashion has had us all in a chokehold for quite some time now, and the runways today resemble twenty years ago more than they did ten, McCall also points out how these looks are in lind with certain trends today, including statement tights ,which have re-entered the fashion conversation. (See from the spring 2027 collections: Jil Sander, Marc Jacobs, Lii, and more.) “Festive tights were a Gossip Girl signature, and that’s a trend that’s stuck around for a few winters now, whether it’s a patterned style or a monochromatic moment,” she says. But still, if you’re looking for something a little less uptown, she recommends channeling one of Serena van der Woodsen’s many silky jewel-toned frocks and tapping into the “lingerie-as-daywear” redux. Somehow, Gossip Girl’s Thanksgiving episodes are a time capsule that captures how all great fashion eventually comes back around.

#6590. This $20 Gadget Is My Grandpa’s Secret To Making Big-Batch Potatoes For The Holidays

It looks a little ridiculous, but I can’t stop watching it work.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

If you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

Mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up new recipes.

Since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

#6589. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6587. 37 Thanksgiving Cocktails and Drinks for Every Guest

Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle. There are the cranberry, apple, and maple flavors we crave this time of year, plus big-batch drinks that won’t keep you playing bartender all afternoon. We’re talking freezer-ready martinis, bourbon punch, and a cranberry mule that guests can spike themselves. After all, your to-do list is long enough.

And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether. When dinner gives way to dessert, warm up with a hot buttered rum, mulled wine, or spiced apple cider. Just don’t forget to set out a few Thanksgiving appetizers while you’re at it.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

We love a Paper Plane as much as the next discerning cocktail drinker, but shaking them up one at a time? Hard pass. Batch the bourbon, Aperol, and amaro for this Thanksgiving cocktail ahead, then stir in the lemon juice and water about an hour before serving.

The “upside-down” refers to the inverted ratio of gin and vermouth in these martinis (not what they’ll do to you). The result is a lighter-drinking cocktail you can batch ahead and stash in the freezer until guests arrive.

All the steeped, spiced flavors you love in a hot toddy, with none of the warmth. This icy twist keeps pre-dinner cocktail hour refreshingly chill. Relatives, take note.

Apple cider, tart cranberry juice, and spicy ginger ale give rum punch a seasonal makeover. Make the cranberry-studded ice cubes ahead of time; they’ll keep the punch cold and make each glass look party-ready.

Sure, a cold beer works fine while you're watching football or tending the turkey fryer. But a pitcher of crisp Mexican lager punched up with margarita citrus makes the occasion feel a little more festive. For another low-effort beer cocktail, try a Spaghett—just lager, Aperol, and lemon.

For a big-batch cocktail with a distinctly autumnal spin, combine rum with dry hard cider and fruit. Prepare the rum base ahead, but save the bubbly cider until just before serving to preserve its fizz.

Bourbon, cognac, floral Earl Grey tea, and an herb-honey syrup make a party-ready punch. For an eye-catching presentation, add an ice ring decorated with lemon slices and rosemary sprigs.

Mezcal, orange liqueur, honey, and chocolate bitters make a lightly smoky cocktail that's particularly good with dessert. Even better, you can batch eight servings and stash them in the freezer up to two weeks ahead. No last-minute shaking required.

Feeling a little gung-ho about Christmas’s fast approach, are we? A big-batch punch packed with cranberry, citrus, nutty sherry, and warming spices makes a delicious bridge between Thanksgiving and the winter holidays.

A seasonal riff on the French 75 swaps gin for bourbon and adds a homemade pear syrup spiced with cinnamon, ginger, and cloves. We like it for a sparkling toast before dinner or alongside pie afterward.

The season of Hallmark’s flannel-clad himbos calls for a drink to match. Enter this lower-ABV sipper made with apple cider and amaro. A little bitter, a little sweet, and just fizzy enough—rather like the male lead in whatever movie “your aunt” is watching.

Homemade cranberry-thyme syrup gives this sparkling cocktail its ruby-red glow. A little Campari adds a pleasantly bitter edge, while Champagne makes it worthy of a holiday toast. The syrup can be prepared up to two weeks ahead.

If you want to start Thanksgiving with a little bubbly, this three-ingredient, lower-ABV aperitif is a fine place to begin. The recipe serves four, and the ginger syrup can be made well in advance.

Replace the gin in a classic Negroni with sparkling wine and you’ve got a lighter, fizzy aperitif. The bubbles mellow Campari’s bitter edge, making this a friendly introduction for the Negroni-curious.

Two ingredients, one very good drink. Fino sherry and ginger ale make a lightly boozy, pleasantly dry cocktail with just enough ginger bite.

Botanical gin, bittersweet grapefruit, and sparkling sake make a bubbly cocktail that’s bright enough to cut through a rich Thanksgiving spread. It serves six, so you can pour a round without mixing drinks one by one.

We love a margarita riff no matter the season. Ginger and rosemary bring a distinctly autumnal edge to this fizzy version, with just enough sparkle to make it feel like a holiday toast.

No punch bowls, cocktail shakers, or complicated mixology required for this two-ingredient drink. You’ve got better things to do between hosting duties and getting all those Thanksgiving sides to the table.

A lower-ABV sipper is your friend during a long day of polite frivolities. The Adonis sounds hella sexy, and we love the earthy nuttiness of sherry and sweet vermouth, made spritzy with club soda.

On a holiday where cranberries overflow-eth, pour a drink to match. Tart, citrusy, and just sweet enough, this vodka cocktail gets its signature pink hue from cranberry juice. A bright counterpoint to all that rich Thanksgiving food.

A classic old-fashioned needs just bourbon or rye, sugar, and bitters. Making drinks for a crowd? Follow our big-batch old-fashioned method to prep ahead and avoid playing bartender all Thanksgiving.

Think of this as an apple-brandy riff on the Manhattan. Sweet vermouth rounds out the fruit’s warmth, making this a particularly fitting fall cocktail.

Not quite a whiskey sour, not quite a cider cocktail, this autumnal drink mixes apple brandy with lemon and orange juices, maple syrup, and a dusting of nutmeg. It tastes like fall without leaning too heavily on baking spices.

Impress your whiskey-loving dad with a Prohibition-era cocktail he may not have heard of. Juicy grapefruit and floral honey give bourbon a bright, citrusy lift, just as winter citrus season is getting underway.

Bourbon, lemon juice, and simple syrup make a tart, boozy drink that’s just sweet enough. It’s ideal for anyone with a minimally stocked bar and a preference for the classics.

Think of the Boulevardier as the Negroni’s bourbon-loving cousin. Whiskey takes the place of gin, bringing warmth and richness to the bittersweet combination of Campari and sweet vermouth. A fine choice for sipping before dinner.

A smoky mezcal cocktail with Earl Grey tea syrup and grapefruit liqueur, this bright, aromatic margarita riff is an intriguing choice for Thanksgiving brunch—or for guests who prefer tequila to bourbon at cocktail hour.

A homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail a distinctly Thanksgiving twist. Lime juice keeps it tart, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim adds a fragrant finish. Make the jam ahead to streamline cocktail hour.

Whether for your Thanksgiving pregame or tomorrow morning’s hair of the dog, a well-made Bloody Mary is always welcome. Worcestershire, horseradish, hot sauce, and fresh lemon give this savory classic its signature kick.

A packed to-do list is no match for this make-ahead drink. Simmer red wine, cider, fruit, and spices ahead of time, then add tawny port and gently reheat when your guests arrive. Keep it warm in a slow cooker for self-service away from the kitchen.

We’d welcome a pot of mulled apple cider at any fall gathering. It’s nonalcoholic, serves a crowd, and fills the kitchen with the scent of warming spices. Guests can add a tipple of brandy, bourbon, Calvados, or rum if they wish.

Can’t decide between hot cider and spice-rich chai? Have both. This cozy, nonalcoholic drink brings tea and warming spices to apple cider, making it a particularly good companion for a second slice of pie.

For those who’d rather drink their Thanksgiving dessert, a warm mug of dark rum, butter, sugar, and spices delivers the goods. It’s rich, fragrant, and an excellent reason to linger at the table after the pie plates are cleared.

Blood orange, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves make this sweet-tart, nonalcoholic drink feel right at home on Thanksgiving. Prepare the shrub ahead, then top with sparkling water when guests arrive.

Who says a nonalcoholic spritz can’t have a little attitude? A bittersweet alcohol-free aperitif and a splash of olive brine give this savory, citrusy drink plenty of complexity. Serve it very cold, with an olive garnish.

Green tea, lemon juice, fresh mint, and honey make a soothing tonic after the Thanksgiving bacchanal. Alcohol-free on its own, it can take a splash of mezcal if anyone wants to steer it into cocktail territory.

Spiced maple syrup and cranberry juice reimagine the typical Moscow mule as a Thanksgiving drink that skips the vodka. Note that Angostura bitters contain alcohol; for a completely alcohol-free version, use an alternative like All the Bitter.

Thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the big turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. We’ve got some clever, simple shortcuts to help you whip up appetizers that will impress your guests without adding to your stress.

Whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another big family meal.

Having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

It’s a tail as old as time: It’s right before Thanksgiving dinner, and your guests don’t want a full meal but are feeling a little peckish. Try a bird of a different feather this year, and serve this festive and impressive fruit and cheese display as the centerpiece of your holiday app table.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. Preparing these potato skins is simple; all you need for this recipe are Thanksgiving leftovers and a few additional pantry staples: potatoes and cheddar cheese.

It’s hard to find a party appetizer that’s more beloved than a cheese log—or its alternate form, the cheese ball. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

These are a fan favorite every fall. They always disappear within minutes, probably because the combo of salty, creamy brie, sweet-tart cranberry sauce, and crunchy pecans is PERFECT.

Fall desserts may get all the attention once autumn comes around, but I'm here to say that seasonal appetizers deserve their share of the spotlight—especially these adorable pizza-stuffed pumpkins. Stuffed with creamy ricotta, these biscuit-based bites are baked to golden perfection before being brushed with a flavor-packed garlic butter.

Just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after the big meal.

Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce

Stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple. The only thing better? MORE. STUFFING. Enter this bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce (just cranberry sauce, honey, and Dijon).

Even if you're not serving turkey this Thanksgiving doesn't mean you can't get in on the theme. Enter: this adorable cheeseball. We used carrots, pecans, pretzels, and bell peppers to create the iconic look, but feel free to substitute them with different ingredients for what you have on hand. Serve it with crackers and use the decorations as dippers too!

These sweet potato bites have a crunchy, herbaceous crust, with a sweet, silky inside that, when topped with a light drizzle of honey, will have you craving them again and again. Once you bite through the crust, the sweet potato mixes with that melted, nutty Gruyère for a dream flavor combination that works SO well.

Cranberry brie bites are by far one of our favorite appetizers for the holidays, but jalapeño poppers also have place in our hearts too... So why not combine them? The spice of the jalapeño goes so well with the tart cranberries.

To make these, we stuff baby bella mushrooms with garlicky, herby breadcrumbs and plenty of cheese. Stuff them ahead of time and bake them off when you're ready for the most Thanksgiving-friendly appetizer ever.

Pull-apart bread reaches a whole new level, thanks to brie and cranberry sauce. Use your favorite homemade sauce recipes, but store-bought works too if you're short for time.

Little puff pastry squares get topped with caramelized onions and a little crumbled goat cheese for an easy appetizer that always wows. The final step is a light drizzle of honey for that salty sweet combination everyone will love.

If you’re a fan of our cranberry brie bites, we’ve got news for you: There’s a new app in town, and it’s inspired by another fan fave, baked feta pasta. These features the flavors you know and love, all nestled into bite-sized cups of golden crescent roll dough.

There's something very classic about the crescent roll dough flavor, so we tend to gravitate toward it, but puff pastry or even biscuit dough should both work here, too.

Think this sounds like a strange combo? You've gotta trust us on this one. If the aroma of toasted puff pastry, roasted apples, and nutty cheddar cheese doesn’t wake up your spirit… we're not sure what will.
